# Taking Money in Vietnam: Stripe, PayPal, SePay, and a Provider-Agnostic Billing Core

*Why Notopia bills through a Stripe sandbox it can never take live, why PayPal "works in Vietnam" but not in VND, and how the billing service is shaped so the payment provider can be swapped later.*

Written with AI during billing-03 (October 2026). Provider facts were checked against their docs at that time. Re-check them before acting on this.

***

## The Situation

Notopia is a Vietnamese team selling a SaaS subscription priced in **VND** (Plus 49,000 ₫/month, Pro 99,000 ₫/month, Pro lifetime 2,490,000 ₫). We want what every SaaS wants:

* hosted checkout, so we never touch card numbers;
* **automatic renewals** (monthly / yearly);
* plan changes and card updates without building our own UI;
* refunds through an API (cancel now, duplicate checkout, lifetime upgrade);
* webhooks so our database follows what happened.

Stripe does all of this out of the box. Here's the catch.

***

## Stripe: Perfect API, Wrong Country

Stripe doesn't onboard businesses registered in Vietnam. An account can be created and the **sandbox (test mode) works fully**, but activating live payments requires a business entity and bank account in a supported country (Singapore and the US are the usual workarounds, with real legal and tax overhead).

VND itself isn't the problem: Stripe supports VND as a presentment currency, as a **zero-decimal currency** (`49000` means 49,000 ₫, not 490.00). Only the merchant's country blocks us.

**Decision: build on Stripe sandbox now.** It's the reference implementation of the model we want, it lets us demo the whole flow end to end, and the billing core is written against our own port, not against Stripe.

***

## PayPal: "Supports Vietnam" ≠ "Supports VND"

Both of these are true at once, which is the confusing part:

1. **PayPal supports Vietnam as a country.** A Vietnamese person or business can open a PayPal account, send money, and receive payments.
2. **PayPal does not support VND as a currency.** The [PayPal currency code list](https://developer.paypal.com/reference/currency-codes/) has 24 currencies (USD, EUR, JPY, SGD, THB, PHP, MYR, …) and VND isn't one of them.

"Country supported" means *who* can hold an account. "Currency supported" means *what an order, subscription plan, or balance can be denominated in*. A Vietnamese merchant on PayPal therefore:

* prices and charges in USD (or another listed currency);
* holds a USD balance in PayPal;
* withdraws to a Vietnamese bank account, converted to VND, paying a conversion spread (commonly reported around 3–4%) plus a withdrawal fee. Users report Vietnamese banks only accepting the payout into a VND account.

Why no VND? PayPal hasn't published a reason. The usual factors for a currency being left out are foreign-exchange regulation (the dong is a managed, not freely convertible, currency, and cross-border flows are controlled by the State Bank of Vietnam), low transaction volume for PayPal in that currency, and settlement partnerships. Treat that as context, not as PayPal's stated reason.

**What this means for us:** PayPal is a real option for *international* customers paying in USD, not for Vietnamese customers expecting ₫ prices. Its API also lacks a few things Stripe gives us:

| Need                                     | PayPal                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Recurring billing                        | ✅ Products + Billing Plans + Subscriptions                                                                |
| Refund API                               | ✅ Refund a capture, with an idempotency request id                                                        |
| Webhooks                                 | ✅ Verified with the verify-webhook-signature API                                                          |
| Customer object                          | ❌ The subscriber is a PayPal account, not a customer we own                                               |
| Hosted portal (change plan, update card) | ❌ We'd build the plan change ourselves with "revise subscription"                                         |
| Change the paying card/person            | ❌ The card belongs to the subscriber's PayPal account. Changing payer means cancelling and re-subscribing |
| VND                                      | ❌                                                                                                         |

Go SDK: [`github.com/plutov/paypal/v4`](https://github.com/plutov/paypal) (community, maintained, covers subscriptions, plans, refunds and webhook verification).

***

## SePay: Built for VND, Built Differently

[SePay](https://docs.sepay.vn/) is Vietnamese and VND-native, but it's a different *kind* of product. It has two layers:

### 1. Bank-transfer reconciliation (the original SePay)

SePay watches **your own bank account** and calls your webhook whenever money arrives. Customers pay by scanning a **VietQR** code in their banking app. The QR encodes the amount and a payment code (e.g. `SEVN63DC8E5C`) in the transfer description, and you match that code to an order.

* Money lands directly in our bank account. There's no intermediate wallet and no card gateway fee.
* Webhook payload: `id`, `gateway`, `transactionDate`, `accountNumber`, `code`, `content`, `transferType` (`in`/`out`), `transferAmount`, `referenceCode`, …
* Webhook auth: API key (`Authorization: Apikey …`), HMAC-SHA256, or OAuth2. The receiver must answer `200/201` with `{"success": true}` within 30 s. Failed deliveries retry 7 times on a Fibonacci backoff, for up to 5 hours.
* Deduplicate on `id`, the same idea as our `processed_provider_events`.

### 2. SePay Payment Gateway (newer)

[developer.sepay.vn](https://developer.sepay.vn/en/cong-thanh-toan/gioi-thieu) adds an order-based gateway: VietQR, NAPAS QR, and **international cards (Visa / Mastercard / JCB with 3-D Secure, through VPBank + Mastercard MPGS)**. You create an order, get a payment link or QR code, the customer pays, SePay sends an **IPN**, and the browser comes back to your `return_url`. There's a sandbox (`pgapi-sandbox.sepay.vn`), Basic Auth with `merchant_id:secret_key`, and Node.js / PHP SDKs (no official Go SDK, but the REST API is small).

### What SePay doesn't have (not found in the docs, October 2026)

* **No recurring billing / saved-card auto-charge.** Every payment is a customer action.
* **No refund API.** A bank transfer refund is another bank transfer, made by a person.
* **No hosted customer portal.**

So SePay is **pull** (the customer pays each time we ask), whereas Stripe and PayPal are **push** (the provider charges a saved method on schedule). That's the important difference for our design, more than the API shapes.

***

## Side by Side

|                                  | Stripe             | PayPal              | SePay                                  |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Live merchant in Vietnam         | ❌                 | ✅                  | ✅                                     |
| Charge in VND                    | ✅ (zero-decimal)  | ❌                  | ✅                                     |
| Automatic renewals               | ✅                 | ✅                  | ❌ (we send a new QR/link each period) |
| Refund API                       | ✅                 | ✅                  | ❌ (manual bank transfer)              |
| Hosted plan change / card update | ✅ Customer Portal | ❌                  | ❌                                     |
| Webhooks + dedup id              | ✅ signed          | ✅ verified via API | ✅ API key / HMAC, `id`                |
| Sandbox                          | ✅                 | ✅                  | ✅ (gateway) / transaction simulator   |
| Go SDK                           | ✅ official        | community           | none (REST)                            |

***

## How the Billing Service Is Shaped Today

The domain and use cases already don't care who the provider is:

```
controller/http/webhook.go  ──► Cmds.CompleteCheckout{SessionID}       (Stripe-specific inbound adapter)
                            ──► Cmds.SyncSubscription{ProviderSubscriptionID}
                            ──► Cmds.SyncRefund{ProviderRefundID}

app/  ── PaymentProvider (port) ──► infra/payment/stripe (the only stripe-go import besides webhook.go)
domain/ Subscription, Refund, BillingAccount: provider ids are plain strings,
        state arrives as ProviderSnapshot / PaymentInfo
```

What already makes a swap cheaper:

* **Fetch-and-sync webhooks.** A webhook is only a signal carrying an id; the handler reads the current state back from the provider. That works for any provider, including SePay's "money arrived" event.
* **Idempotency is ours.** `processed_provider_events` dedups by event id, and refunds carry our own `refund:{id}` key. Every provider in the table gives us an id to dedup on.
* **Entitlements never ask the provider.** `ResolveEntitlements` reads only our database. Other services call gRPC, which never reaches Stripe.
* **Money is `{Amount int64, Currency string}`** in the smallest unit. VND has zero decimals, USD has two, so a USD provider means changing the seed prices, not the code.

Where it's still Stripe-shaped:

* `PaymentProvider` has 17 methods and assumes provider-managed renewals, a customer object, a hosted portal, saved payment methods, and a refund API. PayPal fails 3 of those and SePay fails all 5.
* The webhook controller is Stripe-only (signature check, event names). That's fine as long as each provider gets its **own inbound adapter**, all calling the same commands.

***

## The Provider-Agnostic Design (When We Need It)

**Not now.** We stay on Stripe sandbox and don't add abstractions for a provider we haven't picked. When a second provider becomes real, this is the plan.

### 1. Split the port by capability

```go
// Every provider
type PaymentProvider interface {
    CreateCheckout(ctx, CheckoutInput) (CheckoutLink, error)     // hosted page / payment link / VietQR
    GetCheckout(ctx, id string) (CheckoutSessionResult, error)
    PaymentForRef(ctx, ref string) (domain.PaymentInfo, error)
}

// Optional: provider charges a saved method on schedule (Stripe, PayPal)
type RecurringBilling interface {
    GetSubscriptionSnapshot(ctx, id string) (domain.ProviderSnapshot, error)
    SetCancelAtPeriodEnd(ctx, id string, cancel bool) error
    CancelSubscriptionNow(ctx, id string) error
    PeriodPayments(ctx, id string, start, end time.Time) ([]domain.PaymentInfo, error)
}

type Catalog interface { CreatePrice(...); ArchivePrice(...) }                // Stripe products/prices, PayPal plans; SePay: none (amount per order)
type Refunds interface { CreateRefund(...); GetRefund(...) }               // Stripe, PayPal
type CustomerPortal interface { CreatePortalSession(...); CreatePortalConfiguration(...) } // Stripe
type PaymentMethods interface { SetDefaultPaymentMethod(...); DetachPaymentMethods(...) }  // Stripe
```

Use cases check the capability (`if r, ok := provider.(Refunds); ok`) or take it as a dependency. When it's missing, they fall back to the merchant-managed path below.

### 2. Two renewal modes in the domain

|                          | Provider-managed (Stripe, PayPal)             | Merchant-managed (SePay)                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Who knows the period end | the provider, applied with `ApplySnapshot`    | **us**: `Subscription` advances its own period                                                                                                 |
| Renewal                  | provider charges, webhook says `invoice.paid` | our cron creates a **renewal invoice** N days before the period end, sends the VietQR/link by email or in-app, and the SePay IPN marks it paid |
| Unpaid                   | provider retries, `past_due`                  | our grace period (`BillingPolicy.PastDueGraceDays` already exists), then `canceled`                                                            |
| Cancel at period end     | provider flag                                 | just don't issue the next invoice                                                                                                              |

The `Subscription` aggregate gains a `RenewalMode` and an `Invoice` child (amount, due date, payment code, status). Everything downstream (entitlements, gRPC, notifications) stays the same, because it already reads only `Status` / `Plan` / `CurrentPeriodEnd`.

### 3. Manual refunds as a first-class status

Without a refund API, a `Refund` stays `pending` and shows up in an **admin queue** with the payer's bank details. An admin makes the transfer and marks it `succeeded` with the bank reference. The reconcile cron already retries `pending` refunds with no provider id; for manual providers it simply skips them.

### 4. One inbound adapter per provider

```
POST /billing/webhooks/stripe  → verify Stripe signature  → Cmds.*
POST /billing/webhooks/paypal  → verify via PayPal API    → Cmds.*
POST /billing/webhooks/sepay   → API key / HMAC           → Cmds.MarkInvoicePaid / CompleteCheckout
```

Each is a separate public Traefik route, just like today's Stripe one.

### 5. Record the provider on the account

Add `provider` to `billing_accounts` (and to `subscriptions` and `prices`, since provider price ids differ). This lets two providers coexist during a migration: existing Stripe subscriptions run until their period ends, and new checkouts go to the new provider. Routing comes from the account's provider, not from a global switch.

***

## Recommendation

1. **Now:** Stripe sandbox, as built. It's the most complete model and proves the domain.
2. **First live provider for Vietnamese customers:** SePay (VND, money straight to our bank, cards through the gateway), with merchant-managed renewals and manual refunds. That's the design work above, mostly in the domain plus a renewal cron, not in the adapter.
3. **International customers in USD:** PayPal, or Stripe through a foreign entity if the team ever has one. It reuses the provider-managed path that already exists.

Until step 2 is scheduled, the only rule is the one we already follow: **nothing outside `infra/payment/<provider>` and that provider's webhook adapter imports a payment SDK.**

***

## Sources

* PayPal currency codes: <https://developer.paypal.com/reference/currency-codes/>
* PayPal in Vietnam (user reports, unofficial): <https://www.expat.com/en/forum/asia/vietnam/543698-how-do-paypal-work-in-vietnam.html>
* VND withdrawal costs (third-party guide): <https://vaultleap.com/blog/receiving-usd-payments-in-vietnam-the-complete-guide-2026-2>
* plutov/paypal Go SDK: <https://github.com/plutov/paypal>
* SePay docs: <https://docs.sepay.vn/>, webhooks: <https://docs.sepay.vn/tich-hop-webhooks.html>
* SePay Payment Gateway: <https://developer.sepay.vn/en/cong-thanh-toan/gioi-thieu>

# Casbin Remembers, the Database Changes

*Why a casbin enforcer doesn't see policy rows written by anyone else, and what that means for seeding and for running more than one authorization instance.*

Written with AI during billing-03, October 2026. Not fixed yet; this is the problem statement for a later phase.

***

## How the Enforcer Holds Policy

The authorization service checks permissions with a casbin `TransactionalEnforcer` backed by Postgres (gorm adapter). At startup it calls `LoadPolicy()` once: every row of `casbin_rule` is read into memory, and the `g` rows are turned into the in-memory role graph (see [the role manager story](./casbin-role-manager-clobber.md)).

After that, **every `Enforce` call reads memory only**. The database is touched only when *this* enforcer writes (`AddPolicy`, `RemoveGroupingPolicy`, …): it updates its memory and saves the row, through autosave.

```
process A: memory ◄── LoadPolicy() at start ── casbin_rule ──► LoadPolicy() at start ──► memory :process B
           A writes → A memory + DB                              B never hears about it
```

Casbin doesn't poll or listen to the database. A row written by someone else stays invisible until the process reloads.

***

## Where It Bites

### 1. A separate seed process

If `policy.csv` sync moves out of the service into `cmd/authorizationseed` (planned), the seed writes `p` rows straight into the database. A running authorization instance keeps answering from its old matrix until it restarts. A new permission (say `billing_manage`) is **denied** by already-running pods even though the row exists.

Workable rule for now: **seed first, then start or restart authorization.** In Kubernetes that's a seed Job before the rollout, and a pod that finds the matrix missing reports "not ready" through its startup probe so it gets restarted, instead of serving wrong answers.

### 2. More than one authorization instance

This one already exists in principle. Instance A handles `UpdateWorkspaceMembers` and writes the new `g` row; instance B still has the old role graph. A user just added to a workspace gets `403` whenever their request lands on B, until B restarts. Removing a member is worse: B keeps **allowing** them.

Today we run one instance, so nobody has seen it. Scaling authorization horizontally without fixing this would be a security bug.

***

## Ways Out

| Option              | How                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Trade-off                                                                  |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Single instance     | Keep `replicas: 1`                                                                                                                                                                                                          | No HA; the restart rule still applies to seeding                           |
| Periodic reload     | `e.LoadPolicy()` every N seconds                                                                                                                                                                                            | Simple, but stale for up to N seconds, and a full reload each time         |
| **Watcher (Redis)** | [`casbin/redis-watcher/v2`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/casbin/redis-watcher/v2): `e.SetWatcher(w)`; every write publishes on a Redis channel, and other instances run their update callback (classically `LoadPolicy()`) | Needs Redis (authorization has none today); near-instant                   |
| Watcher (Postgres)  | [`IguteChung/casbin-psql-watcher`](https://beta.pkg.go.dev/github.com/IguteChung/casbin-psql-watcher) over `LISTEN/NOTIFY`, also implements incremental `WatcherEx`                                                         | No new infrastructure; community-maintained, check casbin v3 compatibility |

A watcher only fires for writes that go **through an enforcer with the watcher set**. A seed binary would have to set the same watcher, or the running instances would still need a restart after seeding.

***

## Takeaways

* A casbin enforcer is a cache of the policy table with no invalidation by default.
* "Row exists in the database" ≠ "permission granted": check `Enforce` on the instance that serves traffic.
* Before running more than one authorization instance, add a watcher (Redis or Postgres `LISTEN/NOTIFY`), and make the seed binary notify it too.

---

---

# The Helper Enforcer That Erased Everyone's Membership

*How a "harmless" temporary casbin enforcer, built only to parse a CSV, silently replaced the real enforcer's role manager, and why every workspace member got `403` after a restart.*

Written with AI during billing-03, October 2026. Fixed in `8e55c60d`, tests added in `f85c26e5`.

***

## The Symptom

During the billing end-to-end run, the authorization service was restarted, and suddenly:

```
GET /note/workspaces/{id}/tree        → 403
GET /billing/workspaces/{id}/entitlements → 403 user 112 lacks billing permission
```

The user was the workspace **owner**. The membership row was sitting right there in the authorization database:

```
g, user:112, owner, workspace:01a13526-…
```

Restarting with `APP_ENV=production` instead of `development` seemed to "fix" it, so at first it looked like a dev-only fixtures problem. It wasn't. It was worse.

***

## A 60-second Casbin Primer

Our model (`internal/authorization/app/model.conf`):

```ini
[request_definition]
r = sub, dom, obj, act          # user, workspace, object type, action

[policy_definition]
p = sub, obj, act               # role, object class, action

[role_definition]
g = _, _, _                     # user → role, inside a workspace (domain)
g2 = _, _                       # object type → object class

[matchers]
m = g(r.sub, p.sub, r.dom) && g2(r.obj, p.obj) && r.act == p.act
```

There are two kinds of data:

| Rows                    | Example                           | Where it lives                   | Changes                                          |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `p` (permission matrix) | `p, owner, workspace, read`       | `policy.csv` (static)            | when we change what a role may do                |
| `g2` (object classes)   | `g2, note, workspace_item`        | `policy.csv` (static)            | rarely                                           |
| `g` (memberships)       | `g, user:112, owner, workspace:W` | **database**, written at runtime | every time someone joins, leaves or changes role |

The important bit for this story: casbin does **not** answer `g(...)` by scanning `g` rows. When policies are loaded, it builds an in-memory graph called the **role manager** (`RM`) out of the `g` rows, and `g(user, role, domain)` asks that graph.

```
model["g"]["g"]  ──►  Assertion { Policy: [...g rows...], RM: *RoleManager }
                                                      ▲
                                   Enforce() → g() asks this
```

The `g` rows are the data; the role manager is the index built from them. If you lose the index, the data is still in the database, but every check says "no".

***

## The Code That Did It

The service has the static matrix in an embedded `policy.csv` and needs to push it into the database on startup. Casbin has no "load policies from a string into my existing enforcer" helper. Its file adapter reads from disk paths only, and the string adapter is an adapter, not a loader. So a helper was written that looked perfectly reasonable:

```go
// policyloader.go (old)
func LoadPoliciesFromString(enforcer *casbin.TransactionalEnforcer, csv string) error {
    tempAdapter := stringadapter.NewAdapter(csv)
    tempModel := enforcer.GetModel()                                   // ← same model object
    tempEnforcer, err := casbin.NewTransactionalEnforcer(tempModel, tempAdapter)
    …
    policies, _ := tempEnforcer.GetPolicy()
    enforcer.AddPoliciesEx(policies)                                   // copy rows across
    …
}
```

The idea: let a throwaway enforcer parse the CSV (it understands `p`, `g`, `g2` lines), then copy the rows into the real one. The throwaway enforcer is never used again, so what could go wrong?

***

## What Casbin Does When You Create an Enforcer

`casbin.NewTransactionalEnforcer(m, adapter)` → `InitWithModelAndAdapter` (casbin v3.11.0, `enforcer.go`):

```go
e.model = m          // keeps the *same* model you passed
…
e.initialize()       // → initRmMap()
…
e.LoadPolicy()
```

and `initRmMap` (`enforcer.go:585`):

```go
for ptype, assertion := range e.model["g"] {
    …
    assertion.RM = <new empty role manager>   // writes onto the assertion object
    e.rmMap[ptype] = assertion.RM
}
```

`enforcer.GetModel()` returns the real enforcer's model, so `assertion` here is the **real enforcer's `g` assertion**. Creating the helper enforcer replaced the real enforcer's role manager with a brand-new, empty one. Then the helper loaded `policy.csv`, which has no `g` rows, so that new role manager stayed empty.

```
before:  real enforcer ─► model["g"]["g"].RM = {user:112 → owner @ W, …}   (built from DB)
helper:  NewTransactionalEnforcer(sameModel, csvAdapter)
after:   real enforcer ─► model["g"]["g"].RM = {}                            (empty)
```

Every `g(user, role, workspace)` now returned false. Every permission check failed. The rows were still in Postgres, and the policy list in memory still contained them; only the index was gone.

### "But casbin's LoadPolicy copies the model"

That was the first theory, and it's half right. `LoadPolicy` does work on `model.Copy()`, so loading doesn't mutate the shared model's policy rows. But `Assertion.copy()` copies the `RM` field **by pointer** (`model/assertion.go`), and `initRmMap` runs before `LoadPolicy` anyway, directly on the shared assertions. Copying the model doesn't protect the role manager.

***

## Why It Looked Like a Dev-Only Bug

Startup in `internal/authorization/server.go`:

```go
a.BootStrapPolicies(ctx)            // always
if cfg.AppEnv == development {
    a.LoadFixtures(ctx)             // dev memberships from policy_fixtures.csv
}
```

* **Before the billing work:** `BootStrapPolicies` used `AddPolicies` directly (no helper), and only `LoadFixtures` went through `LoadPoliciesFromString`. Production never touched the helper; development did, through fixtures. That matches "dev broken, prod fine". We couldn't reproduce the exact development failure afterwards: in a repro, the fixtures' `g` adds rebuilt the role links and masked the problem. Either way, only the path that went through the helper misbehaved.
* **After `24c6f124`:** to stop the hardcoded list drifting from `policy.csv`, `BootStrapPolicies` was switched to the same helper. Now **production** clobbered the role manager on every start. In development the fixtures' `g` adds happened to rebuild the links and mask it.

In both versions the root cause was the same: building a second enforcer on the live model.

The bootstrap test passed the whole time, because it only checked `HasPolicy(...)`, which reads the policy rows that were still there. It never called `Enforce`, which is the only thing that uses the role manager.

***

## The Fix

Don't build a second enforcer. Parse the CSV into a **standalone** model and apply the rules to the real enforcer through its normal API (`internal/authorization/app/policysync.go`):

```go
func parsePolicyCSV(csv string) (model.Model, error) {
    m, _ := model.NewModelFromString(ModelConf)       // fresh model, owns its own assertions
    for line := range strings.SplitSeq(csv, "\n") {
        line = strings.TrimSpace(line)
        if line == "" || strings.HasPrefix(line, "#") {
            continue
        }
        if err := persist.LoadPolicyLine(line, m); err != nil {   // casbin's own CSV line parser
            return nil, err
        }
    }
    return m, nil
}

func syncPolicies(e *casbin.TransactionalEnforcer, csv string, prune bool) error {
    desired, _ := parsePolicyCSV(csv)
    p, _ := desired.GetPolicy("p", "p")
    if prune { /* RemovePolicies(current p rows not in csv) */ }
    e.AddPoliciesEx(p)                                  // adds only missing rows
    for _, pt := range []string{"g", "g2"} {
        rules, _ := desired.GetPolicy("g", pt)
        e.AddNamedGroupingPoliciesEx(pt, rules)         // never removes g rows
    }
    return nil
}

func (a *App) BootStrapPolicies(ctx) error { return syncPolicies(a.Enforcer, PolicyCSV, true) }
func (a *App) LoadFixtures(ctx) error      { return syncPolicies(a.Enforcer, PolicyFixturesCSV, false) }
```

`persist.LoadPolicyLine` is the same function casbin's adapters use to read CSV lines, so we get casbin's own parsing without casbin's enforcer setup. Nothing touches the real enforcer's assertions except its own API.

What `policy.csv` means now:

* It is the **single source of truth** for `p` and `g2`.
* Every start adds missing rows and **removes `p` rows no longer in the CSV**, so deleting a permission from the file deletes it from every database.
* `g` rows (memberships) are never removed: they're runtime data.

***

## The Tests That Would Have Caught It

1. **Enforce after restart.** In a file-backed sqlite database, persist a runtime membership, create a *new* enforcer on the same database (a restart), run only `BootStrapPolicies`, then assert `Enforce(user, workspace, "workspace", "read") == true`. This failed on the old code with "persisted membership must survive bootstrap".
2. **Prune.** A stale `p` row in the database that isn't in `policy.csv` disappears after bootstrap, and running bootstrap twice is harmless.
3. **Same matrix, both paths.** `TestModels` (36 permission cases) now runs twice: once with casbin's string adapter reading the CSV directly, once with `BootStrapPolicies` + `LoadFixtures` syncing into sqlite. Both must give identical answers.
4. **Parser.** Comments, blank lines, whitespace, `p`/`g`/`g2` rows, the embedded files (16 `p`, 2 `g2`), and an unknown rule type (`g3`) must error.

***

## Takeaways

* In casbin, **`g` rows are data and the role manager is the index**. A check can fail with the data intact. Test with `Enforce`, not `HasPolicy`.
* **Never pass `enforcer.GetModel()` to another enforcer constructor.** Enforcer setup writes role managers onto the model's assertions, so the two enforcers end up sharing, and overwriting, them.
* To load policy text, parse with `persist.LoadPolicyLine` into a model from `model.NewModelFromString`, then use `AddPoliciesEx` / `AddNamedGroupingPoliciesEx` / `RemovePolicies` on the real enforcer.
* A restart is a test case: write a test that persists data, builds a fresh process-like instance, and checks behaviour, not rows.

# The Documentation Pages That Wouldn't Disappear

*Why publishing PR previews changed how we deploy production documentation.*

Written with AI, November 2026. The preview implementation requires `nx-github-pages` 1.3.1;
the dependency update supersedes PR #185.

## One Branch, Two Kinds of Content

Notopia publishes its documentation and API reference from the `gh-pages` branch. A production
build belongs at the branch root and is served under `/notopia/`. A pull request preview belongs
under `pr/<number>/` and is served under `/notopia/pr/<number>/`.

That shared branch gives us two requirements that pull in opposite directions:

* A production deployment must replace the old production site, including deleting pages that
  no longer exist in the new build.
* The same deployment must leave the `pr/` directory alone, so it does not erase other people's
  previews.

Publishing the build as a complete replacement satisfies the first requirement but loses the
previews. Keeping everything from the old branch protects previews but also keeps obsolete pages.

## The Ghost Page

We looked at `nx-github-pages` 1.3.1, which supports both preview deployments and scheduled preview
cleanup. Its documentation recommends `syncWithBaseBranch` to preserve previews during production
deployments.

The [1.3.1 deploy executor][executor] builds a fresh Git history from the output directory and
merges the existing `gh-pages` branch into it. The default merge favors new files when both
histories have a conflicting file. But a file present only in the old branch is not a conflict:
Git can retain it in the merge. The executor then uses a force-push.

For example:

```text
Old gh-pages:  index.html  retired-guide.html  pr/123/index.html
New build:     index.html
Merged result: index.html  retired-guide.html  pr/123/index.html
```

The preview survived, but the deleted guide did too. It could remain available at its old URL
until someone explicitly removes it. The plugin's [README][readme] describes synced production
deploys as merging rather than force-pushing; the published executor source still invokes
`git push -f`.

This is about what the current site serves, not about erasing Git history: removing a page from the
branch tip does not guarantee that previously published content is gone from history, caches, or
other copies.

## What We Chose

We kept the plugin for preview publishing and age-based preview cleanup. For production,
`scripts/publish-docs.sh` clones the existing `gh-pages` branch, removes the old production files
while preserving `.git` and `pr/`, copies in the new build, and pushes a normal commit. It rejects
a production build that itself contains a top-level `pr` directory, because that path is reserved
for previews.

The normal push also rejects a conflicting update instead of overwriting it. Production, preview,
and cleanup jobs share a non-cancelling concurrency group, but a writer outside that group could
still race; in that case the failed production deployment needs to be rerun.

A disposable Git remote test exercised the important case: two preview directories survived a
production redeploy, while an old production page disappeared. Live preview comments and scheduled
cleanup still need verification on GitHub.

## What Else Made Previews Work

The deployment directory is only half the problem. VitePress, diagrams, the API site, and search
must all use the preview prefix when the site is built. `DOCS_BASE` supplies that prefix, and the
docs, API, and combined page build cache keys include it. Otherwise an Nx cache hit could restore
a production build into a preview, or the reverse.

Preview cleanup is age-based rather than PR-state-based. The plugin uses the most recent Git
commit author timestamp for a preview directory, so a preview for an open PR can expire; a
subsequent PR update recreates it. An unchanged deploy does not refresh its timestamp.

## Takeaways

* A merge that preserves unrelated preview directories can also preserve deleted production files.
* A shared publishing branch needs both a reserved preview path and coordinated writers.
* A build-time URL prefix is part of the build's cache identity.
* Check the published executor's behavior as well as its documentation before relying on
  deployment guarantees.

[executor]: https://github.com/AgentEnder/nx-github-pages/blob/293f6bdec51acde86982c0ffb5fbc6d80e957c44/packages/nx-github-pages/src/executors/deploy/executor.ts

[readme]: https://github.com/AgentEnder/nx-github-pages/blob/293f6bdec51acde86982c0ffb5fbc6d80e957c44/README.md

# Follow-up (2026-10): blocknote 0.55, transitive bundling, and a container that actually boots

> Follow-up to [`nestjs-bundling-otel.md`](./nestjs-bundling-otel.md). Read that first for the *why* of
> the CJS + `ExternalizePlugin` + `keepBundled` design. This doc only records what changed on top of it
> and what was verified.

***

## 0. TL;DR

| Question                             | Answer                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Did blocknote fix its broken `.cjs`? | **No.** `@blocknote/core@0.55.0` still throws `te.default.extend is not a function` under plain `require()`. The `keepBundled` hack is **still required.** |
| Upgraded?                            | `@blocknote/*` 0.50.0 → **0.55.0**; `@nestjs/*` 11.1.x → **11.2.7** (single version, enforced by `overrides`).                                             |
| Was the shipped design correct?      | **Not in Docker.** It only worked under `nx run` (the `@nx/js:node` executor). A plain `node main.cjs`, and the Docker image, crashed. Fixed.              |
| NestJS 12?                           | **Not yet** — see §6.                                                                                                                                      |

***

## 1. Re-test of the blocknote CJS build (§4.1 of the old story)

Bare-node repro in a scratch dir with `@blocknote/core@0.55.0` + `@blocknote/server-util@0.55.0`:

```
require('@blocknote/core')        → 💥 te.default.extend is not a function
require('@blocknote/server-util') → 💥 te.default.extend is not a function
exports["."] = { import: ./dist/blocknote.js, require: ./dist/blocknote.cjs }   (unchanged)
```

No upstream issue/PR/release note mentions fixing it (searched `TypeCellOS/BlockNote` issues, PRs, and
0.51–0.55 release notes). `@handlewithcare/prosemirror-inputrules` is still `0.1.4` (ESM-only). So
`@blocknote/*` + the prosemirror cluster **must stay bundled**.

***

## 2. Blocknote 0.50 → 0.55 migration

| Release | Change                                                                                                                                                                     | What we did                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 0.51    | Markdown ↔ HTML rewritten; ~100 deps (the `unified`/`remark`/`mdast`/`hast` stack) removed from core                                                                       | Nothing — `blocksToMarkdownLossy` (search-worker) and the seed markdown parsing still typecheck/test green                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| 0.52    | **Yjs decoupled**: `collaboration` option must be wrapped in `withCollaboration()` from `@blocknote/core/yjs`; `yjs`/`y-prosemirror`/`y-protocols` became *optional* peers | Wrapped options in `packages/ui/src/components/editor-core.tsx` and `apps/test-editor/src/app/app.tsx`. `CollaborationUser` moved `@blocknote/core/extensions` → `@blocknote/core/yjs` (`packages/lib/src/block-note/collab-user.ts`). Verified pnpm still links `yjs`/`y-prosemirror`/`y-protocols` into core |
| 0.53    | `@blocknote/shadcn` uses base-ui instead of radix                                                                                                                          | No code change needed; `web` + `test-editor` build                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

Note: core also ships a `./y` entry for **Yjs 14** (`@y/y`, `@y/prosemirror`). We are on Yjs 13 / Hocuspocus,
so we use `./yjs`.

***

## 3. The latent bug: transitive deps of bundled packages were external

### 3.1 Symptom

The old static check (§8 of the old story) was run from the *workspace*, where pnpm + the Nx executor make
almost anything resolvable. Run against the built file directly:

```
node apps/document/dist/main.cjs   →  Error: Cannot find module 'orderedmap'
```

and in a simulated/real Docker install, 15 externals were unresolvable:

```
orderedmap rope-sequence w3c-keyname tabbable fast-equals fast-deep-equal use-sync-external-store
emoji-mart @emoji-mart/data async-mutex crossws kleur  (+ subpaths)
```

### 3.2 Cause

`keepBundled` matches by **request name**. `prosemirror-model` is bundled, but its own
`require('orderedmap')` is a different request that matches nothing → externalized. Under pnpm isolated,
`orderedmap` only exists in `.pnpm/prosemirror-model@x/node_modules/`, never in the app's top-level
`node_modules` (nor in the pruned Docker install, which only hoists the app's **direct** deps). This was
true on 0.50 as well — not caused by the upgrade.

### 3.3 Fix (`ExternalizePlugin`, both apps)

```ts
const keepExternal: RegExp[] = [/^jsdom(\/|$)/];
// ...
if (keepExternal.some((re) => re.test(request))) return callback(undefined, `commonjs ${request}`);
return contextInfo?.issuer?.includes('/node_modules/') || keepBundled.some((re) => re.test(request))
  ? callback()
  : callback(undefined, `commonjs ${request}`);
```

**"If the importer is already-bundled third-party code, bundle what it imports too."** Because only the
`keepBundled` cluster's node_modules code is ever *in* the bundle, this gives the full transitive closure
of that cluster — not the one-level issuer regex that failed in old Attempt 3. Workspace libs
(`@notopia-uit/*`) resolve to `packages/…` (symlinks resolved), so their backend imports (`@nestjs/*`, …)
stay external and OTel-patchable.

`jsdom` is the one exception (old §4.2 — bundling drops `xhr-sync-worker.js`), so it is forced external and
added as a **direct dependency** of both apps so the pruned install puts it on the top-level path.

### 3.4 What got bundled additionally (measured from the source maps, old rule vs new rule, both on 0.55)

|                                       | `document`                                                                                                                                                                                                | `search-worker`                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `main.cjs`                            | 4.8 MB → **5.5 MB**                                                                                                                                                                                       | 4.3 MB → **4.9 MB**                                                               |
| node_modules packages in bundle       | 43 → 57                                                                                                                                                                                                   | 38 → 49                                                                           |
| **Newly bundled**                     | `orderedmap` `rope-sequence` `w3c-keyname` `tabbable` `fast-equals` `fast-deep-equal` `use-sync-external-store` `emoji-mart` `preact` `@parcel/runtime-js` `@swc/helpers` `async-mutex` `crossws` `kleur` | same minus `async-mutex` `crossws` `kleur` (those come from `@hocuspocus/server`) |
| **No longer bundled** (reverse)       | none                                                                                                                                                                                                      | none                                                                              |
| Externals (`require()` in `main.cjs`) | 38 → **22**, 0 unresolvable                                                                                                                                                                               | 25 → **12**, 0 unresolvable                                                       |

Build time (`nx run document:build --skip-nx-cache`, 2 runs each): old ≈ 11.9 / 12.8 s, new ≈ 13.7 /
11.6 s — **within noise.** All newly bundled packages are small editor/view leaf deps.

No OTel-instrumented package moved into the bundle.

***

## 4. Docker / Nx fixes (all pre-existing, found while verifying)

| Problem                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Fix                                                                                                                                                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `docker:build` depended on `build` only (`prune` commented out: "It got nx error"). `dist/pnpm-lock.yaml` references `file:./workspace_modules/...` which was never copied → `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` failed. **The image did not build.**                                                                                            | Re-enabled `"prune"` in `docker:build.dependsOn` (both `project.json`). The old Nx error does not reproduce on Nx 23.2.1.                                                     |
| `CMD ["node", "main.js"]` but the build emits `main.cjs`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | `CMD ["node", "main.cjs"]` (both Dockerfiles)                                                                                                                                 |
| Pruned lockfile mixed `@nestjs/core@11.2.3` with `@nestjs/common@11.1.21` → `Cannot find module '@nestjs/common/decorators/http/sse-signal.decorator'`; after bumping, `@openapitools/openapi-generator-cli` (pins `@nestjs/common@11.1.17`) leaked a second copy → `Nest can't resolve dependencies of the TypeOrmCoreModule (…, ModuleRef)` | Catalog `@nestjs/*` → `^11.2.7`, plus `overrides: { "@nestjs/common": "catalog:", "@nestjs/core": "catalog:" }` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` → exactly one version workspace-wide |
| `uuid` imported by `apps/document/src/document/document.service.ts` but not declared (phantom dep via the root `package.json`)                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Added `uuid` to `apps/document` deps. Root `package.json` and `apps/search-worker` (only `seed/transform.ts` uses it) moved `uuid` to `devDependencies`                       |

### 4.1 `.proto` files at runtime

> Deep dive: [`nestjs-grpc-proto-loader.md`](./nestjs-grpc-proto-loader.md). No `.proto` files are needed,
> but the `@grpc/proto-loader` *package* is required eagerly by Nest.

Not needed. The gRPC clients (`apps/document/src/{note,authorization}/*.module.ts`) pass the ts-proto
generated `packageDefinition` (`NoteServiceService`, `AuthorizationServiceService` from `@notopia-uit/pb`)
directly — no `protoPath`, so `@grpc/proto-loader` is never used and no `.proto` file must be shipped.
If someone switches to `protoPath`, the `.proto` files must be copied into the image (`/proto/` is in
`.dockerignore`).

***

## 5. Verification (what "works" means now)

1. `nx run-many -t typecheck test -p packages/ui packages/lib packages/lib-server document search-worker test-editor` ✅
2. `nx run-many -t build -p web test-editor` ✅, `nx lint` ✅
3. `nx run-many -t docker:build -p document search-worker` ✅
4. Static resolve check **inside the container** (every `require("x")` in `/app/main.cjs` must resolve): 0 unresolvable for both.
5. Boot probe in the container (`--env-file apps/<app>/.env`, `OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug`, no local DB/Kafka):
   * `document`: reaches `ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5434` (Postgres) — expected; patched `grpc http kafkajs pg pino`.
   * `search-worker`: `Starting Nest application…` → Kafka connect retry — expected; patched `kafkajs pino`.
   * The patched set equals `OTEL_NODE_ENABLED_INSTRUMENTATIONS`' default in `apps/*/src/otel.ts`
     (`grpc,http,kafkajs,pino,pg,runtime-node`). The richer list in the old story came from the local
     env enabling more.

**The probe that matters is now the container one**, not `nx run`, because the Nx executor masks
resolution failures.

```bash
cat > tmp/document/resolve-check.cjs <<'EOF'
const fs=require("fs"),{createRequire,isBuiltin}=require("module");
const f="/app/main.cjs";const src=fs.readFileSync(f,"utf8");
const names=new Set([...src.matchAll(/require\("([^"./][^"]*)"\)/g)].map(m=>m[1]).filter(n=>!isBuiltin(n)));
const r=createRequire(f);const bad=[...names].filter(n=>{try{r.resolve(n);return false}catch{return true}});
console.log("externals:",names.size,"unresolvable:",bad.join(", ")||"none");
EOF
nx run-many -t docker:build -p document search-worker
for img in document search-worker; do docker run --rm -v $PWD/tmp/document/resolve-check.cjs:/check.cjs:ro $img node /check.cjs; done
```

***

## 6. NestJS 12 — not now

12.1.2 is out. Ecosystem peers mostly allow it (`@nestjs/config@12`, `@nestjs/typeorm@12`,
`nestjs-otel@8.1`, `nestjs-pino@5`), but:

* **All Nest 12 packages ship as ESM** (`"type": "module"`). Our CJS bundle would load them via
  `require(esm)`. That works on Node 25, but require-in-the-middle can't usefully patch a frozen ESM
  namespace, which breaks the premise of old §2. `nestjs-core`/`express` instrumentation is not in our
  default enabled list today, so the immediate loss is small. Still, it needs re-validating, and is
  probably the push toward the swc transpile-only / `--import` hook direction (old §12).
* `@nx/nest@23.2.1` peers `@nestjs/* <12`.
* `@openapitools/openapi-generator-cli` pins `@nestjs/common` 11.x internally. Our new `overrides` would
  force it onto 12. That needs testing, or scoping the override.
* The `typescript-nestjs-server` generator output (`packages/api-document-nestjs-server`) has not been
  checked against 12.

Treat it as its own migration, with the container probe in §5 as the acceptance test.

url: /notopia/pr/428/developer/story/nestjs-bundling-otel.md
