# Bundling the NestJS apps (document / search-worker): OpenTelemetry logs, CJS, and the externals split

> **Update 2026-10:** see [`nestjs-bundling-otel-2026-10-blocknote-055.md`](./nestjs-bundling-otel-2026-10-blocknote-055.md).
>
> **Update 2026-11:** `inquire-shim.js` removed, see [Changelog](#changelog).
> blocknote 0.55 still ships a broken `.cjs` (hack still needed). Transitive deps of the `keepBundled` cluster
> are now bundled too (`contextInfo.issuer` rule, §10 below is outdated), and the Docker image was fixed and
> verified. The §8 `nx run` probe masks resolution failures; use the container probe there instead.

> **Single consolidated story.** Supersedes and merges the two former docs
> (`js-bundling-rspack.md` — the OTel-logs / bundle-size investigation, and
> `nestjs-cjs-vs-esm-bundling.md` — why ESM output is a dead end). Read top to
> bottom. It is self-contained: a fresh session should be able to understand both
> *what* the build does and *why every alternative was rejected* without re-deriving
> any of it. Long on purpose — the reasoning is the point.

***

## 0. TL;DR — the final design (✅ shipped)

The two NestJS apps (`apps/document`, `apps/search-worker`) are bundled with **rspack to CommonJS**
(`main.cjs`, `isEsm = false`). The externals rule is:

> **Externalize everything by default; bundle ONLY the blocknote editor cluster** (the packages that
> cannot survive a native `require()`), plus the workspace libs and the tiny transpile runtimes.

Concretely, `keepBundled` (bundled) is:

```
@blocknote/*  prosemirror-*  @handlewithcare/*  @tiptap/*
yjs  y-protocols  y-prosemirror  lib0
react  react-dom  scheduler  @floating-ui/*
@bufbuild/protobuf
@notopia-uit/*           (workspace libs — they import @blocknote)
tslib  @swc/helpers      (transpile runtimes)
```

**Everything else is external** — all backend infra (`@nestjs/*`, `rxjs`, `typeorm`, `express`, `pg`,
`kafkajs`, `@grpc/*`, `@aws-sdk/*`, `@smithy/*`, `pino`, `@opentelemetry/*`, `jose`, `marked`, `zod`, …)
**and** blocknote's well-behaved dual-package leaf deps (the `unified`/`remark`/`mdast`/`hast` markdown
stack). They all load fine via native `require()`.

Results (verified):

|                                             | before                  | after                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `apps/document/dist/main.cjs`               | **98 MB** dev           | **~4.6 MB**                                                                                           |
| `apps/search-worker/dist/main.cjs`          | (similar)               | **~4.2 MB**                                                                                           |
| OTel instrumentations that patch (document) | `http`/`dns`/`net` only | `pino`, `pg`, `kafkajs`, `grpc`, `nestjs-core`, `express`, `router`, `aws-sdk` (+ `http`/`dns`/`net`) |

Why this shape and not any of the half-dozen alternatives we tried is the rest of this document.

***

## 1. The goal: emit OpenTelemetry **logs**

The apps already emitted traces and metrics, but **never logs**. The log pipeline is:

```
nestjs-pino → pino → @opentelemetry/instrumentation-pino → OTel Logs SDK → OTLP exporter
```

`@opentelemetry/instrumentation-pino` attaches a `pino.multistream` destination that forwards every log
record to the OTel Logs SDK. **It attaches that destination by patching the `pino` module via
require-in-the-middle (RITM) at `require('pino')` time.** No patch → no bridge → no logs.

### Things we ruled out (do NOT chase again)

These were investigated and proven harmless; the missing logs were *only* the pino patch:

* **Duplicate `@opentelemetry/api-logs` (0.214 vs 0.215).** Harmless. Both register under the same global
  symbol `Symbol.for('io.opentelemetry.js.api.logs')` with the same `API_BACKWARDS_COMPATIBILITY_VERSION = 1`,
  so the global LoggerProvider is shared. (`sdk-node@0.215` pulls api-logs 0.215; `instrumentation-pino@0.60.0`
  pins `^0.214.0`, which for 0.x means `<0.215`.)
* **`pino-pretty` custom `stream:`.** Does not block log-sending. `instrumentation-pino` wraps the existing
  destination via `multistream([{stream: yourPretty}, {stream: otelStream}])` — both run.
  (Source: `instrumentation-pino/build/src/instrumentation.js` ~lines 60–86.)
* **`@opentelemetry/sdk-node@0.215`.** Auto-creates the LoggerProvider from `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` (default
  otlp) when no `logRecordProcessors` are passed (`sdk.js` ~lines 145–157, 265). The pipeline already exists;
  the only missing piece was the pino patch.

### The root cause in one line

rspack **bundled `pino` inline**, so there was **no runtime `require('pino')`** for RITM to intercept →
instrumentation never patched → no logs. In the original 98 MB all-bundled build, only the *core-module*
instrumentations patched (`http`, `dns`, `net`); none of `pino`/`pg`/`kafkajs`/`grpc`/`nestjs-core` did.

**The fix direction is therefore forced: the OTel-instrumented packages must be EXTERNAL** (real
`require()`s), not inlined. Everything below is the consequence of pursuing that without breaking the apps.

***

## 2. Why CJS output, not ESM (a settled dead end)

Before discussing *which* packages to externalize, settle the module format, because "just switch the bundle
to ESM" comes up and is wrong. The apps emit **`main.cjs` (`isEsm = false`) deliberately.**

### 2.1 RITM only intercepts CommonJS `require()`

The whole logs fix relies on RITM hooking `Module._load` and wrapping each subsequent `require('pino')`.
In an **ESM** bundle, external deps are pulled with `import`, which RITM cannot intercept. OTel's ESM path
needs **import-in-the-middle (IITM)**, a different mechanism hooking Node's ESM loader via
`module.register()` / `--import`.

### 2.2 A loader hook registered *from inside the graph* is always too late

ESM links **all** static imports before any module body executes (depth-first, post-order). The bootstrap is
load-bearing:

```ts
// apps/*/src/main.ts
import './otel'; // otelSdk.start() → installs the RITM hook
import '@notopia-uit/lib/yjs';
import 'reflect-metadata';
// …then NestFactory.create(...)
```

Under **CJS** this works: `import './otel'` runs `otelSdk.start()` **synchronously first**, and the external
deps are `require()`d **later** (during Nest bootstrap) → intercepted. Under **ESM** in a single bundled
file, the external `import pino` is a top-level import **hoisted above** the inlined `import './otel'` side
effect, so `pino` is linked *before* `otelSdk.start()` runs → nothing left to patch. This is structural, not
incidental.

The only ESM-correct fix is to register the hook at the Node CLI level *before* the graph loads
(`node --import @opentelemetry/instrumentation/hook.mjs`), which means abandoning `import './otel'`-first,
rewiring the `@nx/js:node` run/serve invocation and the Dockerfile entrypoint, **and** trusting
`instrumentation-pino` to patch a CJS `pino` through the CJS→ESM interop under IITM — unproven for this stack.

### 2.3 Concrete ESM breakages already in the code

* `apps/document/src/main.ts` uses `module.hot` / `module.hot.dispose(...)`. `module` is a **CJS-only**
  global; it does not exist in ESM.
* The app `package.json` is `"type": "module"`, but the build emits `.cjs` on purpose (the `.cjs` extension
  forces CJS regardless of `type`). Flipping to `.mjs` re-exposes every issue here.
* The suppressed `Critical dependency` rspack warnings (`typeorm`, `nestjs`, `express`, `app-root-path`,
  `load-esm`) are **dynamic `require(expr)`** inside bundled CJS deps. ESM has no `require`; rspack injects
  `createRequire` shims, but dynamic-expression requires there are fragile.
* `reflect-metadata` ordering and NestJS decorator metadata (`emitDecoratorMetadata`) have extra sharp edges
  under ESM hoisting.
* rspack `experiments.outputModule` + `target: node` + node externals is far less battle-tested than CJS.

### 2.4 ESM doesn't even solve the blocknote crash

ESM's only marginal benefit would be that externalizing blocknote resolves the **import** condition (the good
ESM build) instead of the broken **require** `.cjs`. But we don't need that — we just **keep blocknote
bundled** (§4), which already fixes the crash under CJS. ESM solves nothing CJS doesn't, while costing
§2.1–§2.3.

> **Verdict:** Stay on CJS. Do not re-attempt ESM unless the OTel strategy is first redesigned around a
> `node --import` ESM loader hook and validated end-to-end for pino logs.

***

## 3. How the build is wired (the levers, and the Nx gotcha)

* Each app has `apps/<app>/rspack.config.ts` exporting a config that includes
  `new NxAppRspackPlugin({ ... })` (from `@nx/rspack/app-plugin.js`). `@nx/rspack` is **22.7.5**.
* `NxAppRspackPlugin.apply()` → `applyBaseConfig()`
  (`node_modules/.pnpm/@nx+rspack@22.7.5_*/node_modules/@nx/rspack/src/plugins/utils/apply-base-config.js`).
* **Critical gotcha #1:** `applyBaseConfig` ends with `config.externals = externals;` — a **hard
  overwrite**. Any `externals:` you set directly in the rspack config object is **discarded**. (The repo once
  had a `webpack-node-externals` call in the config; it was dead code for exactly this reason.)
* **Critical gotcha #2 — the `externalDependencies` option is too weak:**
  * default `'none'` → bundle everything (the original bug; pino inlined; 98 MB).
  * `'all'` → uses `webpack-node-externals` scanning `${workspaceRoot}/node_modules`. **Broken under pnpm
    isolated** (app deps aren't in the workspace-root `node_modules`).
  * **array** → Nx pushes a function doing an **exact `ctx.request` match** only
    (`if (externalDependencies.includes(ctx.request)) cb(null, 'commonjs '+request)`). Subpath imports like
    `@aws-sdk/client-s3` or `rxjs/operators` **won't match**, and you can't express "externalize a whole
    scope."

**How we beat both gotchas:** pass `externalDependencies: 'none'` to Nx (so it sets `config.externals = []`),
then install our **own externals function** in a trailing plugin (`ExternalizePlugin`) whose `apply()`
overwrites `compiler.options.externals` **after** Nx ran (it sits later in the `plugins` array). That gives
us a real regex/name-based externals function with full control.

`externalsPresets: { node: true }` stays set, so node builtins are externalized by the preset independently
of our function (our function also lets builtins fall through to be safe).

***

## 4. The blocknote crash — root cause (the pivot of the whole design)

The first instinct ("externalize everything so OTel can patch it") produces a tiny bundle (888 KB) but
**crashes at runtime**:

```
TypeError: h.default.extend is not a function
    at .../@blocknote/core/.../defaultBlocks (Code.extend({...}))
```

`search-worker` crashes identically (it pulls `@blocknote` via `@notopia-uit/lib-server`).

### 4.1 Root-caused with a bare-node repro (supersedes earlier guesses)

The crash is **purely blocknote's broken published CJS build under Node's `require(ESM)` interop.** It is
**NOT** caused by OTel/RITM, **NOT** by rspack, and **NOT** a `.ts`-resolution issue. Proven with plain
`node` (no bundler, no instrumentation):

| Repro                                                           | What Node loads                            | Result                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| `require('@blocknote/core')` (plain node)                       | `dist/*.cjs` (**require** condition)       | 💥 `h.default.extend is not a function` |
| `import` the ESM entry (incl. `ServerBlockNoteEditor.create()`) | `dist/blocknote.js` (**import** condition) | ✅ works                                |

* `@blocknote/core@0.50.0` `exports["."]` = `{ import: ./dist/blocknote.js, require: ./dist/blocknote.cjs }`.
  The **`.cjs` build is broken**; the **`.js` (ESM) build is fine**. `h.default.extend` is blocknote's own
  CJS-interop artifact — a `.default` access on a dep that Node's `require(ESM)` shapes differently. The RITM
  frame in the *original* stack trace was incidental; bare `node` crashes the same way.
* So the lever is **which build loads (ESM good vs CJS broken)**, governed by the **import vs require
  condition**:
  * **Externalize + CJS bundle** → emits `require('@blocknote/core')` → Node picks the **require** condition →
    broken `.cjs` → crash. *(This is why "externalize blocknote" fails.)*
  * **Bundle (rspack)** → resolves via `mainFields: ['module','main']` → inlines the **ESM** build → works.
    It works because it pulls the ESM build, not because rspack "fixes" interop.
* **Upgrade note:** a newer `@blocknote/*` may ship a fixed `.cjs`, which would make plain externalization
  viable. Re-test the bare-node repro after any bump before relying on it.
  *(Re-tested on 0.55.0 in 2026-10: still broken. See the follow-up story.)*

**Conclusion: `@blocknote/*` MUST be bundled.** That single fact is the seed the whole `keepBundled` list
grows from.

### 4.2 The jsdom landmine (the opposite direction)

We use `@blocknote/server-util` → `jsdom`. **BlockNote issue #1939:** *bundling* jsdom bundles its
dynamically-loaded worker file `lib/jsdom/living/xhr/xhr-sync-worker.js`, which rspack doesn't emit →
runtime `Cannot find module './xhr-sync-worker.js'`. So **jsdom must be EXTERNAL** (it's plain CJS, safe) so
Node loads it from `node_modules` and finds the worker. Under our default-external rule this is automatic —
but it's the canonical example that the bundle/externalize decision has failures in *both* directions:

* `@blocknote/core` → **must bundle** (externalizing loads the broken `.cjs`).
* `jsdom` → **must externalize** (bundling drops a worker file).

There is no universally safe default; you maintain an exception list whichever way you point.

***

## 5. The journey: every approach we tried and why it was rejected

This is the heart of the doc. Each attempt taught one fact that constrains the final design.

### Attempt 0 — Bundle everything (the starting state)

* `externalDependencies: 'none'`. `main.cjs` ≈ **98 MB** dev.
* pino inlined → **no logs** (§1). Slow rebuilds.
* ❌ Fails the goal.

### Attempt 1 — Externalize everything (minus workspace libs)

* Bundle shrank to **888 KB** (document) / **72 KB** (search-worker); `pino`/`grpc`/`nestjs-core` patched. 🎉
* But **crashes** on the blocknote broken `.cjs` (§4.1).
* ❌ Proves: you cannot blindly externalize; blocknote (and its ilk) must bundle.
* ✅ Also proved something crucial used later: in that 888 KB build, the app ran **all the way to the
  blocknote crash with no `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`** — i.e. *externalized transitive deps resolve fine at runtime
  in this repo's run setup.* (The nx node executor / pnpm layout makes them resolvable.) Keep this in mind.

### Attempt 2 — Curated externalize **allowlist** (the first thing that worked)

* Externalize only the OTel-instrumented CJS packages:
  document `['pino','pg','kafkajs','@grpc/grpc-js']`, search-worker `['pino','kafkajs']`.
* ✅ Works: boots to DB-retry, no blocknote crash, `pino`/`pg`/`kafkajs`/`grpc` patch. Logs bridge attached.
* ⚠️ Bundle still ≈ 98 MB → slow. **But here we found the real size culprit (below).**

#### 5.a The 98 MB was mostly a **duplicate source map**, not packages

`apps/document` had BOTH `devtool: 'source-map'` **and** a redundant `new rspack.SourceMapDevToolPlugin({})`.
The plugin inlined a **64 MB base64 source-map data URI** into `main.cjs` *on top of* the external
`main.cjs.map` (35.6 MB of actual code + 64 MB inline map ≈ 99.7 MB). `search-worker` never had that plugin.
**Removing it dropped `main.cjs` from 99.7 MB → 35.6 MB** with zero behavior change. *Lesson: measure before
blaming `@aws-sdk`.* (Externalizing `@aws-sdk/*`/`@smithy/*` is a real but secondary win.)

### Attempt 3 — Invert to **default-external + `keepBundled` editor list + issuer fallback**

* Rule: externalize everything except a `keepBundled` regex list (the editor/CRDT stack), plus "bundle
  anything imported *from within* a bundled package" (an issuer-path regex) to drag transitive editor deps in.
* Bundle ≈ **18 MB**. Builds.
* ❌ A static scan of the emitted `require()`s found **41 externalized packages that don't resolve at
  runtime** (`@tiptap/*`, `mdast-util-*`, `micromark-*`, `hast-util-*`, jsdom internals, …). The one-level
  issuer regex only catches direct deps of named packages; deep transitives leak out as broken externals.
  They'd `MODULE_NOT_FOUND` the moment that editor code path runs — *invisible at boot.*

### Attempt 4 — Default-external + **`require.resolve`-based** decision (clever, still wrong)

* Idea: instead of guessing, externalize a package **only if it actually resolves** from the app
  (`createRequire(app).resolve(name)`), else bundle. "Self-validating; MODULE_NOT_FOUND impossible."
* Bundle ≈ **4 MB**. Booted.
* ❌ Two fatal flaws:
  1. **`package.json` fallback false-positives.** `resolve('@tiptap/core')` fails but
     `resolve('@tiptap/core/package.json')` succeeds → marked "resolvable" → externalized → but the real
     `require('@tiptap/core')` at runtime fails (no/blocked main export). Static check still showed **33
     unresolvable**.
  2. **Build-time vs runtime resolution don't match** under pnpm/Nx — the anchor during the build resolved a
     different set than `apps/<app>/dist/main.cjs` sees at runtime. A resolver-based heuristic is unreliable
     here. *Lesson: don't decide externalization by filesystem resolution under pnpm isolated.*

### Attempt 5 — Bundle **only `@blocknote/*`** (+ workspace libs + helpers)

* The minimalist reading of "just bundle the broken one." Bundle ≈ **978 KB** / **604 KB**. 🎉 tiny.
* ❌ Crashes with a *new* error:
  ```
  No "exports" main defined in .../@handlewithcare/prosemirror-...
  ```
  blocknote → `prosemirror-*` → `@handlewithcare/prosemirror-*`, which ships an **ESM-only `exports` map with
  no CJS main**. Externalized, Node's native `require()` of it throws. *Lesson: "bundle only blocknote" is
  impossible — its prosemirror editor cluster contains packages that can't be `require()`d natively, so they
  must bundle with it.*

### Attempt 6 — Bundle the **blocknote editor cluster**, externalize everything else ✅ (FINAL)

* `keepBundled` = blocknote + prosemirror + @handlewithcare + @tiptap + yjs/y-*/lib0 + react/react-dom/
  scheduler + @floating-ui + @bufbuild/protobuf + @notopia-uit/* + tslib/@swc/helpers (§0).
* Externals function is **simple** (no resolver, no issuer): bundle app code / aliases / builtins / the
  `keepBundled` cluster; externalize all else.
* ✅ Bundle ≈ **4.6 MB** / **4.2 MB**. No `Code.extend`, no `No "exports" main`, no `MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, both
  boot. **More** instrumentation patches than ever (because nestjs/express/aws/pg/kafka are now external):
  `pino`, `pg`, `kafkajs`, `grpc`, `nestjs-core`, `express`, `router`, `aws-sdk` + core `http`/`dns`/`net`.

Why bundling fixes both crash classes: rspack reads the package's **`exports`/`mainFields` at build time**
(it understands ESM `exports`), compiles the ESM build in, and there is **no runtime `require()` to fail** —
neither blocknote's broken `.cjs` nor `@handlewithcare`'s missing CJS main is ever hit.

***

## 6. The rule of thumb (how to classify a package)

> **Bundle** a package only if it **cannot survive a native `require()`** under CJS. Two sub-cases:
>
> 1. **Broken require-condition interop** — e.g. `@blocknote/core` (its `.cjs` throws `Code.extend …`).
> 2. **ESM-only / no CJS `exports` main** — e.g. `@handlewithcare/prosemirror-*`, prosemirror view layer;
>    `require()` throws `No "exports" main defined`.
>
> Plus, by extension, anything that *imports* a must-bundle package and would otherwise run that import
> natively (`@notopia-uit/*` workspace libs import `@blocknote`), and singletons that must stay one instance
> while a bundled consumer holds them (`yjs` CRDT identity; `@bufbuild/protobuf` type registry).
>
> **Externalize** everything else — it loads fine natively, keeps the bundle small, and (for the
> OTel-instrumented packages) is the *only* way RITM can patch it. This includes blocknote's own dual-package
> leaf deps (`unified`/`remark`/`mdast`/`hast`), which are well-behaved CJS.

A new editor dep that's ESM-only may occasionally need adding to `keepBundled`. The failure is **loud**
(`No "exports" main` / `Code.extend` at boot) and the fix is **one regex line**. Re-run the §8 probe after any
`@blocknote`/prosemirror bump.

***

## 7. Why a custom externals function, not `webpack-node-externals`

This came up repeatedly; the answer is decisive.

1. **It scans a directory; we must decide by name.** `webpack-node-externals` externalizes "whatever package
   folders exist in a scanned `node_modules`." Under pnpm's **isolated** linker that gives the **wrong answer
   for the single most important package**: `pino` is a *transitive* dep (we depend on `nestjs-pino`/
   `pino-http`/`pino-pretty`, not `pino`), so it isn't a flat entry in `apps/<app>/node_modules` → a dir-scan
   **bundles** it → `instrumentation-pino` can't patch → **no logs**, the exact bug we set out to fix.
   Pointing it at `.pnpm` doesn't help (the folder is `pino@9.x`, which won't match `require('pino')`).
2. **The decision axis is "editor cluster vs backend," a name-based regex set** — independent of pnpm's
   on-disk layout. `webpack-node-externals`' `allowlist` could express the keep-bundled side, but you'd write
   the *same* regex list **and** still be fighting #1. It buys nothing and costs correctness.
3. **Smaller and clearer.** The whole thing is one `keepBundled` array + a ~10-line function. No
   `modulesDir`/`additionalModuleDirs`/`importType` tuning, no dependency on store layout.

Con (honest): a custom default-external means a new ESM-only editor dep could need a `keepBundled` line later
— but `webpack-node-externals` wouldn't save you there either (you'd touch its `allowlist` the same way).

***

## 8. How to verify (the probe — no DB/Kafka needed; we check patching + no crash)

```bash
# Build + size
pnpm exec nx run document:build --no-tui && du -h apps/document/dist/main.cjs

# Patch + boot probe (routes logs to console, silences trace/metric exporters)
OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=console OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=none OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none \
  pnpm exec nx run document:run --no-tui > /tmp/doc.log 2>&1; echo "exit=$?"

grep -aoE "instrumentation-[a-z-]+ Applying" /tmp/doc.log | sort -u          # which patched
grep -aiE 'Code.extend|is not a function|No "exports" main|Cannot find module' /tmp/doc.log  # MUST be empty
grep -aiE "Starting Nest application|Unable to connect to the database" /tmp/doc.log         # booted?
```

> ⚠️ zsh gotcha: write `nx run "${app}:run"`, not `nx run $app:run`. In zsh, `$app:run` triggers the `:r`
> modifier (strip extension) and mangles `document:run` → `documentun` ("Cannot find configuration for task").

* **Good run** = no crash lines; reaches "Starting Nest application…"; for document, `pino`/`pg`/`kafkajs`/
  `grpc`/`nestjs-core`/`express`/`aws-sdk` all show `Applying`. For search-worker: `pino`/`kafkajs`/
  `nestjs-core`/`express`.
* **Non-zero exit is expected** — the app dies in the DB/Kafka connect-retry loop (no local DB/broker). That
  is not a build/instrumentation failure.
* **Static safety check (optional but valuable):** parse the emitted `require("…")` names out of `main.cjs`
  and confirm each resolves from `apps/<app>/dist/main.cjs`; a non-empty "unresolvable" list means an editor
  transitive leaked out as a broken external → add it (or its bundled importer) to `keepBundled`. This is how
  Attempts 3/4 were caught.

> Full end-to-end log *record* emission can't be observed locally (no DB → the app exits before NestJS
> flushes pino; Nest uses `bufferLogs: true`, flushed only after `NestFactory.create()` resolves +
> `app.useLogger(...)`). The instrumentation **patch firing** is the deterministic proof the bridge is in
> place; records follow against a real DB + collector.

***

## 9. Environment / constraints (all verified)

* Monorepo: **Nx + pnpm** (workspace catalog), **rspack** for the NestJS apps; `@nx/rspack` **22.7.5**.
* pnpm uses the **isolated** node-linker (default; no hoist in `.npmrc`). App direct deps are symlinked into
  `apps/<app>/node_modules`; transitive deps live nested in `node_modules/.pnpm`. **A transitive package is
  NOT a flat entry in the app's `node_modules`** — this is why §7 #1 bites and why directory/resolver
  heuristics (§5 Attempts 3–4) are unreliable.
* **Node 25.x** — executes `.ts` via type-stripping and has strict `require(ESM)` interop (the lens through
  which blocknote's `.cjs` breaks).
* `tsconfig.base.json` has `"customConditions": ["@nx/source"]` (TS-solution setup).
* Build runs from the **workspace root** cwd, but **runtime `require()` resolution is anchored at the built
  `main.cjs` location** (`apps/<app>/dist/`). Externalized deps resolve via the app's reachable
  `node_modules`. Attempt 1 verified the broad set resolves at runtime in this repo.
* Runtime image is handled: `NxAppRspackPlugin({ generatePackageJson: true })` emits a pruned
  `dist/package.json`; `prune` / `copy-workspace-modules` targets ship `node_modules` for Docker. The
  generated manifest lists the app's **direct** deps (e.g. `@blocknote/core`, `pino-http`, `@nestjs/*`); their
  transitives are installed by pnpm from that manifest.

***

## 10. The final config (annotated)

`apps/document/rspack.config.ts` and `apps/search-worker/rspack.config.ts` (same shape; search-worker's
`keepBundled` is identical — it also pulls blocknote via `@notopia-uit/lib-server`):

```ts
import { createRequire, isBuiltin } from 'module';
// …

// Bundle ONLY the blocknote editor cluster — packages that cannot survive a native
// require() (broken require-condition interop, or ESM-only / no CJS exports main),
// plus the workspace libs that import them and the tiny transpile runtimes.
// EVERYTHING ELSE is external (backend infra + blocknote's dual-package leaf deps),
// which keeps the bundle small AND lets OTel's require-in-the-middle patch pino/pg/
// kafkajs/grpc/nestjs/express at runtime.
const keepBundled: RegExp[] = [
  /^@blocknote\//,
  /^prosemirror-/,
  /^@handlewithcare\//,
  /^@tiptap\//,
  /^yjs$/,
  /^y-protocols(\/|$)/,
  /^y-prosemirror$/,
  /^lib0(\/|$)/,
  /^react$/,
  /^react-dom(\/|$)/,
  /^scheduler(\/|$)/,
  /^@floating-ui\//,
  /^@bufbuild\/protobuf/,
  /^@notopia-uit\//,
  /^tslib$/,
  /^@swc\/helpers/,
];

class ExternalizePlugin {
  apply(compiler: rspack.Compiler) {
    // Overwrite the externals Nx hard-assigned. Runs after NxAppRspackPlugin
    // because it sits later in the `plugins` array.
    compiler.options.externals = [
      ({ request }, callback) => {
        if (
          !request ||
          /^[./]/.test(request) || // relative/absolute
          request.startsWith('@/') || // alias
          request.startsWith('@database') || // alias
          request.startsWith('#/') || // package imports field
          isBuiltin(request) // node builtins (preset handles too)
        ) {
          return callback(); // → bundle
        }
        return keepBundled.some((re) => re.test(request))
          ? callback() // → bundle the editor cluster
          : callback(undefined, `commonjs ${request}`); // → externalize everything else
      },
    ];
  }
}
```

Plugin order (load-bearing): `NxAppRspackPlugin({ … externalDependencies: 'none' })` **first**, then
`new ExternalizePlugin()`, then the rest.

### 10.1 Bundling-only scaffolding still required

These exist purely because we bundle the editor cluster; keep them:

* `stub.js` — `NormalModuleReplacementPlugin(/file-type$/, …)` stubs `file-type` (ESM-only, pulled by a
  bundled dep).
* `inquire-shim.js` — `NormalModuleReplacementPlugin(/@protobufjs\/inquire/, …)` shims a dynamic
  `require(expr)` so it doesn't warn/break when bundled (`@bufbuild/protobuf` neighborhood).
  **Removed 2026-11**, see [Changelog](#changelog).
* `IgnorePlugin` + the `lazyImports` set — drops optional peer deps (`mysql`, `oracledb`, `ioredis`,
  `class-validator`, etc.) that bundled CJS libs (`typeorm`, `@nestjs/*`) reference behind feature flags.
* `jsdom` is **not** in `keepBundled` (it externalizes by default) — §4.2.

### 10.2 The source-map fix (don't regress)

`apps/document` must **not** carry both `devtool: 'source-map'` and `new rspack.SourceMapDevToolPlugin({})` —
that double-emits a ~64 MB inline source map into `main.cjs` (§5.a). Use only `devtool` (external `.map`).

***

## 11. Files / facts reference

* `apps/document/rspack.config.ts`, `apps/search-worker/rspack.config.ts` — the `ExternalizePlugin` +
  `keepBundled` described in §10.
* `apps/*/src/otel.ts` — NodeSDK + `getNodeAutoInstrumentations()`; sets the enabled-instrumentations default
  (pino included).
* `apps/*/src/main.ts` — `import './otel'` first; `bufferLogs: true`; `app.useLogger(Logger)` after create.
* `apps/*/src/app.module.ts` — `LoggerModule` (nestjs-pino) with a `pino-pretty` stream; `OpenTelemetryModule`
  (nestjs-otel) for metrics.
* Nx externals logic: `@nx/rspack/src/plugins/utils/apply-base-config.js` (`config.externals = externals`
  overwrite; the `externalDependencies` branches).
* Related already-merged OTel work (don't redo): `fix(otel): connect Go traces, emit gin/grpc metrics, and
  enable web OTLP logs`; `fix(document,search-worker): externalize npm deps so OTel can instrument them`;
  `chore: move type express to dev deps in nestjs`; `chore(lib,ui,pb): use peerDependencies for host-provided
  singletons`.

***

## 12. Roads not taken / future directions

* **Proposal: stop bundling, swc transpile-only (`@nx/js:swc`).** NestJS backends are normally not bundled.
  Output your compiled `src/` (a few hundred KB), keep **all** `node_modules` external. Every package then
  loads as authored — no interop landmines, no `keepBundled` list, every instrumentation patches natively, and
  you can delete `stub.js` / `inquire-shim.js` / `IgnorePlugin`. Cost: a real build migration (touch
  `project.json` build target, Dockerfile, the TypeORM migrations path, `mise.toml`, `out-tsc`/`dist`
  assumptions). The runtime `node_modules` is already handled by `generatePackageJson` + prune. **This is the
  cleanest long-term answer** if/when someone wants to invest the migration; the current rspack design is the
  pragmatic in-place fix.
* **Upgrade `@blocknote/*` past a fixed `.cjs`.** If a future release ships a working require-condition build,
  blocknote could be externalized and `keepBundled` could shrink toward empty. Re-run the bare-node repro
  before relying on it.
* **`dependencies`/`devDependencies` split (optional, image size only).** Bundled-only packages
  (`@blocknote/*`, prosemirror, yjs, react…) could move to each app's `devDependencies` so
  `generatePackageJson` stops shipping them in the runtime image. Correctness-neutral (dead weight only);
  **externalized packages must stay in `dependencies`.** Skipped to keep the externals↔manifest coupling out
  of scope.

```
```

***

## Changelog

### 2026-11: removed `inquire-shim.js`

**Previously.** §10.1 listed `apps/document/inquire-shim.js` as required scaffolding: a
`NormalModuleReplacementPlugin(/@protobufjs\/inquire/, …)` that swapped protobufjs's `inquire` helper
(`eval("require")`, which rspack turns into an empty context module) for a static map of `fs`, `path`,
`long` and `buffer`. It existed so that `Root.loadSync` could read `.proto` files from inside the bundle.
The three rspack configs also carried a comment that bundling `@bufbuild/protobuf` "keeps inquire-shim
valid".

**What changed.**

* `@protobufjs/inquire` is gone from the dependency tree. protobufjs 7.6.6 (pulled by
  `@grpc/proto-loader`) and 8.x (direct, upgraded 8.4 → 8.8 in the same cycle) no longer depend on it;
  8.6.1's changelog says "Remove inquire submodule". The replacement regex therefore matched nothing.
* `Root.loadSync` never runs anyway. We pass ts-proto's `packageDefinition` to Nest, so no `.proto`
  file is read at runtime ([`nestjs-grpc-proto-loader.md`](./nestjs-grpc-proto-loader.md)).
* The "keeps inquire-shim valid" comment confused two libraries. `@bufbuild/protobuf` is the ts-proto
  wire runtime; `inquire` belonged to protobufjs.

**Verification.** `document` was built with and without the shim (after the protobufjs 8.8 upgrade):
`main.cjs` and `migrate.cjs` were byte-identical. A baseline on the old deps (protobufjs 8.4.2) had zero
`inquire` references in `main.cjs`. The only output difference: `long` dropped from the generated
`dist/package.json`, because Nx had inferred it solely from the shim's `require('long')`. Nothing in
`document` or `@notopia-uit/pb` imports `long`, and protobufjs still installs it as its own dependency.

**Result.** Deleted `apps/document/inquire-shim.js` and its plugin entry, and dropped the comment from
the `ai`, `document` and `search-worker` rspack configs. `stub.js` and the `IgnorePlugin` set from §10.1
are unchanged. `docs/src/stories/tmp/nestjs-rspack.md` suspects they are unused too, but they have not
been verified.

# NestJS gRPC: no `.proto` files at runtime, but `@grpc/proto-loader` must be installed

> Related: [`nestjs-bundling-otel-2026-10-blocknote-055.md`](./nestjs-bundling-otel-2026-10-blocknote-055.md) §4.1.

## TL;DR

|                                  | Needed at runtime? | Why                                                                                                                     |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `.proto` files                   | **No**             | We pass ts-proto generated `packageDefinition`; Nest never calls `loadSync(protoPath)`                                  |
| `@grpc/proto-loader` **package** | **Yes**            | `ClientGrpcProxy` / `ServerGrpc` `require()` it eagerly in their constructors, used or not; missing → `process.exit(1)` |

## How we configure gRPC

`apps/document/src/{note,authorization}/*.module.ts`:

```ts
transport: Transport.GRPC,
options: {
  package: NOTE_PACKAGE_NAME,
  packageDefinition: { [`${NOTE_PACKAGE_NAME}.${NOTE_SERVICE_NAME}`]: NoteServiceService },
  url: servicesCfg.noteUrl,
},
```

`NoteServiceService` comes from `@notopia-uit/pb` (ts-proto, `outputServices=grpc-js`), a pure-JS
service definition with encode/decode functions. No protobuf schema is parsed at runtime.

## What Nest does (`@nestjs/microservices@11.2.7`)

```js
// client/client-grpc.js — constructor
grpcPackage            = loadPackage('@grpc/grpc-js', ...);
grpcProtoLoaderPackage = loadPackage(protoLoader, ..., () => require('@grpc/proto-loader')); // always
this.grpcClients = this.createClients();   // → loadProto()

// helpers/grpc-helpers.js
function getGrpcPackageDefinition(options, grpcProtoLoaderPackage) {
  ...
  return packageDefinition || grpcProtoLoaderPackage.loadSync(file, options.loader); // loader only if no packageDefinition
}

// @nestjs/common/utils/load-package.util.js
catch (e) { logger.error(`The "${name}" package is missing...`); process.exit(1); }
```

`server/server-grpc.js` has the same eager require. `@grpc/proto-loader` is **not** a peer dep of
`@nestjs/microservices`. It resolves today because `@grpc/grpc-js` depends on it and pnpm's hidden hoist
(`node_modules/.pnpm/node_modules`) makes it reachable. `apps/document` also declares it directly
(since `refactor: move from connectrpc to grpc`), which is what guarantees it lands in the pruned Docker
install. **Keep that direct dep**, even though our code never imports it.

## Upstream history

* [nestjs/nest#8457](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/issues/8457): "provide a packageDefinition option
  instead of providing .proto files". Before this, Nest *did* require `.proto` files.
  * [#8465](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/pull/8465) (2021-11): `packageDefinition` for `ClientGrpc`.
  * [#10530](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/pull/10530) (2023-12): `packageDefinition` for `ServerGrpc`.
* [#12560](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/issues/12560) (closed 2024-11): proto-loader options are
  server-global rather than per-package (related, not our problem).
* No issue found about making the `@grpc/proto-loader` require lazy when `packageDefinition` is used.

## Verified (2026-10)

* A real `ClientGrpcProxy` with `NoteServiceService`, plus a preloaded hook logging every
  `fs.*('*.proto')`, then a `getNoteName` call: it reached the network (`code=14` UNAVAILABLE) with
  **zero** `.proto` accesses. Positive control: `proto-loader.loadSync('proto/note/note.proto')` under
  the same hook logged the reads.
* Inside the `document` image, `@grpc/proto-loader` and `@grpc/grpc-js` resolve from
  `@nestjs/microservices`.
* `/proto/` is in `.dockerignore`, and that's fine. Only switching a module to `protoPath` would require
  shipping `.proto` files (plus `buf/validate`, `google/protobuf` imports).

---

url: /notopia/pr/428/developer/story/nextjs-vercel-otel-compatibility.md

# Next.js OpenTelemetry compatibility

The web app uses `@vercel/otel` for Next.js instrumentation, including its Edge-compatible
registration path. The NestJS services use `@opentelemetry/sdk-node` independently. They run
in separate processes and do not need the same SDK generation.

## Why web has its own catalog

At the time of this change, `@vercel/otel` 2.3.0 declares peer dependencies on OpenTelemetry
SDK 2.x and experimental packages 0.2xx. SDK 2.x requires `@opentelemetry/api` below 1.10;
SDK 3.x requires API 1.10 or newer. A shared catalog would resolve incompatible versions for
one of the apps. The `web-otel` catalog in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` pins web to API 1.9.1,
SDK 2.12.1 and experimental packages 0.223.2. The default catalog tracks SDK 3.x for NestJS.

Web declares the `@vercel/otel` peer packages explicitly so pnpm resolves them as a matching
set. `@opentelemetry/sdk-logs` 0.220 and newer requires
`new BatchLogRecordProcessor({ exporter })`, not the former exporter-only constructor.

`@vercel/otel` 2.3.0 treats the literal `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=false` as disabled. The web
bootstrap temporarily removes that value during synchronous registration and restores it
afterwards. `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true` still disables the SDK.

## Transport and homelab

Web uses OTLP over HTTP/protobuf for both traces and logs. `@vercel/otel` supports HTTP
trace exporters, but not its own gRPC trace exporter. Web's Node.js log exporter uses
`@opentelemetry/exporter-logs-otlp-proto`. The bootstrap rejects unsupported protocols
instead of silently sending to the wrong port. It also allows `http/json` for traces when
logs are independently configured as `http/protobuf`.

The web chart defaults to `otel.protocol: http/protobuf`. Its endpoint must point to an
OTLP HTTP receiver, not a gRPC-only endpoint. The homelab web values use
`http://alloy-alloy.monitoring.svc:4318`. Alloy's homelab `config.alloy` listens for OTLP
HTTP on 4318 and gRPC on 4317; its Helm values expose both ports. Other Notopia services
keep using gRPC on 4317. Alloy forwards traces to Tempo and logs to Loki. These are repository
settings, not proof of the live cluster's configuration.

## Upgrade when Vercel supports SDK 3.x

1. Check the published `@vercel/otel` peer dependencies and its changelog. Confirm support
   for API 1.10+, SDK 3.x, and matching experimental packages; do not infer compatibility
   from a successful install or a version number alone.
2. Update `@vercel/otel` and align web's complete OTel peer and exporter set with that
   supported generation. Remove the `web-otel` catalog only if the web and default catalog
   versions can actually be shared. Keep direct declarations needed for peer resolution.
3. Follow the [OTel JS 3.x migration guide](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-js/blob/main/doc/3.x/migration-guide.md):
   the logs API moves from `@opentelemetry/api-logs` into `@opentelemetry/api`, trace SDK
   packages change, and package export maps replace unsupported deep imports. Review
   Vercel's migration notes and the log processor constructor as well.
4. Check whether the `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=false` workaround is still needed. Remove it only
   after verifying both `true` and `false` against the upgraded package.
5. Inspect the resolved web dependency graph and Next.js peer resolution for mixed or
   unsupported API/SDK versions. Build and lint web, and run its existing tests.
6. With telemetry enabled, send a trace and a log to a real or local OTLP HTTP receiver.
   Verify Next.js request spans, log export, context propagation, and the disabled-SDK path.
   Check the built container and the deployed collector separately; chart rendering alone
   does not establish connectivity or delivery.

See the [NestJS bundling story](./nestjs-bundling-otel.md) for backend instrumentation and
container constraints.

---

---
url: /notopia/pr/428/developer/story/note-workspace-event-sse-issue.md

# The SSE Ghost That Lived After the Request Died

*A story about a goroutine that didn't know when to quit, a pipe that got closed under its feet, and the panic that followed.*

Written, fixed by AI, in commit a9be674771dc -> e023ee0c6609

***

## The Setup

Notopia's note service has a real-time feature: when you open a workspace in the browser, the frontend opens a persistent HTTP connection to `/note/workspaces/:workspaceId/events` and listens for changes — a note was renamed, a folder was moved, someone joined. This is implemented with **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**, a simple standard where the server streams newline-delimited text over a single long-lived HTTP connection.

On the Go side, the API is generated by `oapi-codegen` from an OpenAPI spec. The spec declares the endpoint with `text/event-stream` response type, and the tool generates a server interface, request/response types, and a strict handler dispatcher. The actual streaming logic — what to send, when, and how to keep the connection alive — is left for us to implement.

The first implementation worked, until it didn't.

***

## The Crime Scene

The symptoms appeared in the logs like this:

```
time=2026-05-23T07:03:04.031Z level=WARN msg="failed to send heartbeat" error="failed to write heartbeat SSE event: io: read/write on closed pipe"
time=2026-05-23T07:03:04.031Z level=DEBUG msg="sent heartbeat"
```

Two lines. Same millisecond. One says it failed. The other says it succeeded. That is already suspicious — a log that contradicts itself is usually a goroutine that didn't know it was the ghost at its own funeral.

Then, when the client disconnected and reconnected, the server crashed hard:

```
[GIN-debug] [WARNING] Headers were already written. Wanted to override status code 200 with 500

panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=0x57c592]

goroutine 1701 [running]:
bufio.(*Writer).Flush(0x1?)
    net/http/server.go:405 +0x39
net/http.(*response).FlushError(...)
net/http.(*response).Flush(...)
github.com/gin-gonic/gin.(*responseWriter).Flush(...)
github.com/notopia-uit/notopia/internal/note/controller/http.(*workspaceEventSSESender).sendHeartBeat(...)
    internal/note/controller/http/sse.go:86 +0x2a3
```

`bufio.(*Writer).Flush(0x1?)` — that `0x1?` in the argument is Go's way of saying the pointer was effectively nil. The server process exited.

***

## The Architecture of the Old Code

To understand what went wrong, we need to understand how the old code was structured.

### What oapi-codegen generates

For an SSE endpoint, `oapi-codegen` generates two things relevant to us.

**First**, a response type for the 200 case:

```go
type GetWorkspaceEvents200TexteventStreamResponse struct {
    Body          io.Reader
    ContentLength int64
}

func (response GetWorkspaceEvents200TexteventStreamResponse) VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse(w http.ResponseWriter) error {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
    w.WriteHeader(200)

    flusher, ok := w.(http.Flusher)
    if !ok {
        _, err := io.Copy(w, response.Body)
        return err
    }
    buf := make([]byte, 4096)
    for {
        n, err := response.Body.Read(buf)
        if n > 0 {
            w.Write(buf[:n])
            flusher.Flush()
        }
        if err != nil {
            if err == io.EOF {
                return nil
            }
            return err
        }
    }
}
```

The idea here is: you give it an `io.Reader`, it reads chunks from it and writes them to the HTTP response, flushing after each chunk so the client sees data immediately. Simple and elegant for a static body. For a live stream it begs a question: *who is writing to the other end of the pipe?*

**Second**, the strict handler dispatcher:

```go
func (sh *strictHandler) GetWorkspaceEvents(ctx *gin.Context, workspaceId WorkspaceIdPath) {
    // ... build request object ...
    response, err := handler(ctx, request)

    if err != nil {
        sh.options.HandlerErrorFunc(ctx, err)
    } else if validResponse, ok := response.(GetWorkspaceEventsResponseObject); ok {
        if err := validResponse.VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse(ctx.Writer); err != nil {
            sh.options.ResponseErrorHandlerFunc(ctx, err)
        }
    }
}
```

The dispatcher calls your application handler, gets back a response object, then calls `VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse(ctx.Writer)` on it. Everything is synchronous from the dispatcher's perspective — `Visit` runs in gin's handler goroutine and the dispatcher waits for it to return.

### What the old application code did

The old `GetWorkspaceEvents` handler tried to bridge the gap by combining the generated `io.Reader`-based response type with a goroutine that does the actual event pumping:

```go
func (h *StrictHandler) GetWorkspaceEvents(ctx context.Context, ...) {
    c := ctx.(*gin.Context)   // cast to get the ResponseWriter

    eventCh, _ := h.WorkspaceEventHub.Subscribe(ctx, ...)

    r, w := io.Pipe()
    sender := newWorkspaceEventSSESender(ctx, eventCh, w, c.Writer)
    sender.Stream()   // starts a goroutine

    return note.GetWorkspaceEvents200TexteventStreamResponse{Body: r}, nil
}
```

And the `Stream` goroutine:

```go
func (s *workspaceEventSSESender) Stream() {
    ticker := time.NewTicker(30 * time.Second)
    go func() {
        defer ticker.Stop()
        for {
            select {
            case <-s.ctx.Done():
                s.writer.Close()
                return
            case <-ticker.C:
                if err := s.sendHeartBeat(); err != nil {
                    slog.Warn("failed to send heartbeat", ...)
                }
                slog.Debug("sent heartbeat")  // unconditional — runs even on failure
            case evt, ok := <-s.eventCh:
                _ = s.send(evt)  // error discarded
            }
        }
    }()
}
```

Where `sendHeartBeat` wrote to the `io.PipeWriter` and then called `s.flusher.Flush()` — and `s.flusher` was `c.Writer`, the gin `ResponseWriter`.

So at runtime, two goroutines were alive simultaneously:

| Goroutine                       | What it does                                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **A** — gin's handler goroutine | Runs `VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse`: reads from `PipeReader`, writes to `ResponseWriter`, calls `Flush()` |
| **B** — the Stream goroutine    | On each tick or event: writes to `PipeWriter`, calls `Flush()` on the *same* `ResponseWriter`                |

***

## The Bugs

### Bug 1: The mutex that protected nothing important

`workspaceEventSSESender` had a `sync.Mutex`. It was locked inside `send()` and `sendHeartBeat()` around the writes to the `PipeWriter` and the `Flush()` calls. This serialized concurrent calls *within goroutine B*.

But goroutine A — the generated Visit loop — never touched that mutex. It was calling `w.Write()` and `flusher.Flush()` on the same `ResponseWriter` completely independently. The mutex was protecting the wrong thing. The actual shared resource, the `gin.ResponseWriter`, had zero synchronization between the two goroutines.

This is a data race. The Go race detector would have flagged it. On most runs it was fine because the timing worked out — goroutine A was blocked on `PipeReader.Read()` while goroutine B was calling `Flush()`. But "fine most of the time" is exactly how latent concurrency bugs hide.

### Bug 2: The unconditional "sent heartbeat" log

```go
if err := s.sendHeartBeat(); err != nil {
    slog.Warn("failed to send heartbeat", ...)
}
slog.Debug("sent heartbeat")  // always runs
```

`slog.Debug("sent heartbeat")` is outside the error check. It runs whether or not `sendHeartBeat` failed. That is where the contradictory log lines came from — "failed to send heartbeat" followed immediately by "sent heartbeat" at the same millisecond. Not two separate heartbeats. One heartbeat that failed, and then a lie.

### Bug 3: The discarded error

```go
_ = s.send(evt)
```

The error from sending an actual workspace event was silently discarded. If a write failed, the goroutine just moved on, the event was lost, and nobody knew.

### Bug 4: The crash — use-after-free on the ResponseWriter

This is the fatal one. Here is the sequence:

1. Client connects. SSE stream runs normally.
2. **Client disconnects.** Gin cancels the request context — `ctx.Done()` is now ready.
3. In the `select` loop of goroutine B, *both* `ctx.Done()` and `ticker.C` might be ready at the same moment. Go's `select` picks among ready channels uniformly at random.
4. If `ticker.C` wins, goroutine B proceeds to call `sendHeartBeat()`.
5. `sendHeartBeat()` writes to the `PipeWriter`. But by now, goroutine A (the Visit loop) may have returned — the `PipeReader` was closed by `defer closer.Close()`. Writing to a pipe with no reader gives `io: read/write on closed pipe`. The error check catches this and returns early, *before* calling `Flush()`. This is the "failed to send heartbeat" log.
6. *But.* If the pipe write succeeded (maybe the pipe buffer still had space), execution falls through to `s.flusher.Flush()`.
7. Goroutine A has already returned from `VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse`. Gin has logged the completed request (status 200). The `http.response` object is being torn down. The internal `*bufio.Writer` inside it is set to nil during cleanup.
8. `s.flusher.Flush()` → `gin.responseWriter.Flush()` → `http.response.Flush()` → `bufio.Writer.Flush(nil)` → **nil pointer dereference → panic → process exit.**

The goroutine outlived the request it was serving. It held a pointer to a `ResponseWriter` that no longer belonged to it. When it reached out and touched it, the process died.

***

## The Fix: Stop Fighting the Framework

The root cause is the two-goroutine design. The generated Visit method runs in gin's goroutine and owns the `ResponseWriter`. The Stream goroutine runs separately and also touches the `ResponseWriter`. That tension is the source of every bug listed above.

The fix is to stop fighting the framework and work *with* the codegen pattern.

### What the codegen actually offers

The generated strict handler dispatches like this:

```go
} else if validResponse, ok := response.(GetWorkspaceEventsResponseObject); ok {
    if err := validResponse.VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse(ctx.Writer); err != nil {
        sh.options.ResponseErrorHandlerFunc(ctx, err)
    }
}
```

It calls `VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse` synchronously. It waits for it to return. **This is the hook.** If `Visit` blocks, gin's goroutine blocks — and that goroutine is the rightful owner of the `ResponseWriter` for the duration of the request.

The generated `GetWorkspaceEvents200TexteventStreamResponse` is just one concrete type that satisfies the `GetWorkspaceEventsResponseObject` interface. We are not required to use it. We can implement our own type.

### The new implementation

```go
type WorkspaceEventStreamResponse struct {
    ctx     context.Context
    eventCh <-chan app.WorkspaceEvent
}

var _ note.GetWorkspaceEventsResponseObject = (*WorkspaceEventStreamResponse)(nil)

func (r *WorkspaceEventStreamResponse) VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse(w http.ResponseWriter) error {
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
    w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
    w.Header().Set("Connection", "keep-alive")
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)

    flusher, ok := w.(http.Flusher)
    if !ok {
        return fmt.Errorf("response writer does not support flushing")
    }
    flusher.Flush()

    ticker := time.NewTicker(30 * time.Second)
    defer ticker.Stop()

    for {
        select {
        case <-r.ctx.Done():
            return nil
        case <-ticker.C:
            if err := writeHeartBeat(w); err != nil {
                slog.Warn("failed to send heartbeat", slog.Any("error", err))
                return nil
            }
        case evt, ok := <-r.eventCh:
            if !ok {
                return nil
            }
            if err := writeWorkspaceEvent(w, evt); err != nil {
                slog.Error("failed to send event", slog.Any("error", err))
                return nil
            }
        }
        flusher.Flush()
    }
}
```

And the handler becomes:

```go
func (h *StrictHandler) GetWorkspaceEvents(ctx context.Context, ...) (note.GetWorkspaceEventsResponseObject, error) {
    user, ok := commonhttp.UserFromContext(ctx)
    if !ok {
        return nil, errs.Unauthorized
    }

    eventCh, err := h.WorkspaceEventHub.Subscribe(ctx, request.WorkspaceId, user.ID)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, errs.NewInternalErr("failed to subscribe to workspace events", err)
    }

    return NewWorkspaceEventStreamResponse(ctx, eventCh), nil
}
```

No `*gin.Context` cast. No `io.Pipe`. No goroutine. No reference to `c.Writer` that can escape the request lifetime.

### Why this fixes everything

**The concurrent Flush race is gone.** There is only one goroutine that ever touches the `ResponseWriter`: gin's handler goroutine, which is now blocked inside `VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse` running our select loop. Goroutine B no longer exists.

**The use-after-free is gone.** Our `Visit` method runs inside the handler goroutine. When the request ends — either because `ctx.Done()` fires or because a write fails — `Visit` returns, the dispatcher returns, and gin cleans up the `ResponseWriter`. Nothing else holds a pointer to it.

**The misleading log is gone.** Each write attempt has one code path — if it fails, we log and return. There is no unconditional "success" line outside the error check.

**The discarded error is gone.** Both heartbeat and event write errors are logged and cause the loop to exit cleanly.

**The "Headers already written" warning is gone.** When a write fails (client dropped before `ctx.Done()` fired), we return `nil` from `Visit` rather than the error. This prevents the `ResponseErrorHandlerFunc` from trying to write a 500 status on top of an already-started 200 response. The error is logged; gin cleans up normally. SSE disconnections are not application errors.

### A note on the headers

The generated `GetWorkspaceEvents200TexteventStreamResponse.VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse` sets `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and writes the 200 status. But since we implement our own type that satisfies `GetWorkspaceEventsResponseObject`, the generated type's `Visit` is **never called**. The strict handler dispatches directly to our type. We own full responsibility for every header.

This is why the headers in `VisitGetWorkspaceEventsResponse` are not redundant — they are the only place those headers get set. We also add `Cache-Control: no-cache` and `Connection: keep-alive`, which the generated type doesn't include but which are SSE best practice: `no-cache` prevents any proxy from buffering the stream, and `keep-alive` signals the connection intent explicitly.

***

## What the Event Hub Does

The `WorkspaceEventHub` in `internal/note/infra/workspaceevent/workspaceevent.go` is the source of events. It:

1. Publishes workspace change events to a **Redis Stream** — a distributed queue that survives multiple service instances
2. Runs a single internal router goroutine that reads from Redis and fans events out per workspace onto an in-memory `gochannel`
3. When `Subscribe(ctx, workspaceID, userID)` is called, it subscribes to the per-workspace internal topic and returns a `<-chan app.WorkspaceEvent`

The goroutine inside `Subscribe` translates raw Watermill messages into typed `app.WorkspaceEvent` values, skips events from the same user (your own changes don't echo back to you), and drops events when the subscriber's channel buffer is full rather than blocking the fan-out.

The key contract between the hub and the SSE layer: **the returned channel is closed when the context is cancelled.** Our `Visit` loop handles this with `case evt, ok := <-r.eventCh: if !ok { return nil }` — a closed channel means the subscription is done and we exit cleanly.

***

## Lessons

**Codegen is a contract, not a cage.** `oapi-codegen` generates `GetWorkspaceEvents200TexteventStreamResponse` as a convenience for simple streaming scenarios. The real extensibility point is the `GetWorkspaceEventsResponseObject` interface. Implementing that interface on your own type gives you complete control while staying within the framework's dispatch model.

**If two goroutines touch the same `http.ResponseWriter`, you have a data race.** `http.ResponseWriter` is not documented as safe for concurrent use. The `sync.Mutex` in the old code was protecting the wrong level of abstraction — it guarded the PipeWriter but left the ResponseWriter unprotected.

**A goroutine that outlives its request is a ticking clock.** The old Stream goroutine held `c.Writer` — a pointer into gin's request state. Once the request finished and gin began cleanup, that pointer became a landmine. The fix is to ensure the goroutine that drives the SSE loop *is* the request's goroutine, so its lifetime is naturally bounded by the request.

**`select` does not guarantee order among ready channels.** When `ctx.Done()` and `ticker.C` are both ready at the same instant, Go picks one at random. The old code relied on the select eventually picking `ctx.Done()`. It would — eventually. But "eventually" is not the same as "before the next heartbeat tick." This is why the goroutine could call `Flush()` on a cleaned-up `ResponseWriter` even after the context was cancelled.

**Log lines that appear in pairs are a red flag.** "failed to send heartbeat" followed immediately by "sent heartbeat" at the same timestamp is a goroutine saying contradictory things because the success log was placed outside the conditional. If your structured logger shows success and failure for the same operation in the same millisecond, there is a bug nearby.

***

*Written May 2026. The code lives in `internal/note/controller/http/sse.go`.*

# The Docs Build That Lost `useData`

*How a patch bump of `vitepress-openapi` broke page rendering in CI, and why the error pointed at VitePress itself.*

Written with AI, November 2026. Fixed by bundling `vitepress-openapi` for SSR in `docs/.vitepress/config.mts`.

***

## The Symptom

After a Renovate batch, `nx run docs:build:production` failed in CI. The client and server bundles
built fine, then the page-rendering step failed:

```
✗ rendering pages...
SyntaxError: The requested module 'vitepress' does not provide an export named 'useData'
    at loadESMFromCJS (node:internal/modules/cjs/loader)
```

Pagefind looked like the cause because `vitepress-plugin-pagefind` 0.4.26 → 0.4.27 was in the
same batch. It wasn't: that diff only changes scroll handling in `CommandList.vue`.

## Finding It

VitePress deletes `.vitepress/.temp` (the SSR bundle) when the build fails. We preloaded a small
script that made `fs.rm` skip `.temp` paths, so the bundle stayed on disk. `app.js` left only two
third-party imports external:

```
vitepress-mermaid-renderer   → import ok
vitepress-openapi/client     → useData is missing
```

`vitepress-openapi` had moved from 0.2.9 to 0.2.14 in the same batch. 0.2.13 ("theme: follow
VitePress isDark") added this to the client entry:

```js
import { useData } from 'vitepress';
```

Versions 0.2.9 and 0.2.12 have no `vitepress` import.

## Why It Breaks

While VitePress bundles code for SSR, it points `vitepress` at its client runtime, which exports
`useData`. Vite keeps third-party packages external during SSR, though, so Node loads
`vitepress-openapi/client` on its own at render time. Node then resolves `vitepress` through the
package's `exports` and gets the **node** entry, the config/build API, which has no `useData`.

```
bundled code      : 'vitepress' → client runtime   ✓ useData
external package  : 'vitepress' → dist/node/index  ✗ useData
```

## The Fix

Bundle the package so its `vitepress` import goes through VitePress's alias:

```ts
vite: {
  ssr: {
    noExternal: ['vitepress-openapi'],
  },
},
```

Pinning 0.2.12 also works, but it blocks future updates.

## Takeaways

* A VitePress plugin that imports client APIs (`useData`, `useRoute`, …) must be in
  `ssr.noExternal`, or it breaks during the SSR render step only.
* When the SSR bundle fails, keep `.temp` and import each external package in Node to find the
  one that fails.
* A Renovate batch breaks the build as a group. Check every bumped package, not just the one
  that looks most likely.

---

---
url: /notopia/pr/428/developer/story/watermill-event-gaps.md
---

# The Event Processor That Would Have Eaten Every Message

*Why the billing service's Kafka consumers don't use Watermill's CQRS `EventProcessor`, even though the note service does, and the one-line metadata convention that makes the difference.*

Written with AI while building `internal/billing/controller/event` (billing-03, Task 10).

***

## The Setup

Billing has to react to three things that happen in other services:

| Topic                                                          | Publisher          | Billing reaction                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `events.integration.note.workspace.deleted`                    | note (Go)          | Cancel the subscription now, refund the unused part                   |
| `events.integration.authorization.user_workspace_role_updated` | authorization (Go) | If the payer lost the owner role: payer missing, cancel at period end |
| `events.integration.authorization.workspace_member_removed`    | authorization (Go) | Same as above                                                         |

The payload types live once in `api/share/` and are generated into `pkg/api/share`. Our services are on Watermill, and the note service already consumes Kafka. Copying its pattern was the obvious move.

Note's event controller uses Watermill's [CQRS component](https://watermill.io/docs/cqrs/), which looks great:

```go
eventProcessor.AddHandler(cqrs.NewEventHandler(
    "NotifyWorkspaceRenamedHandler",
    e.app.Events.NotifyWorkspaceRenamed.Handle, // func(ctx, *WorkspaceRenamed) error
))
```

You get typed handlers, no `json.Unmarshal` boilerplate, and a topic derived from the Go type. The obvious question in review: *why doesn't billing do this too?*

***

## How the EventProcessor Actually Routes

The EventProcessor doesn't just decode the payload into the handler's type. Before it calls your handler, it checks the message's identity, in `components/cqrs/event_processor.go` (v1.5.2):

```go
expectedEventName := p.config.Marshaler.Name(initEvent)

return func(msg *message.Message) error {
    messageEventName := p.config.Marshaler.NameFromMessage(msg)

    if messageEventName != expectedEventName {
        if !p.config.AckOnUnknownEvent {
            return fmt.Errorf("received unexpected event type %s, expected %s", ...)
        } else {
            // log "Received different event type than expected" and ack
            return nil
        }
    }
    // ... unmarshal + call handler
}
```

And `JSONMarshaler.NameFromMessage` is:

```go
func (m JSONMarshaler) NameFromMessage(msg *message.Message) string {
    return msg.Metadata.Get("name")
}
```

So the processor routes by a **`name` metadata header**. The topic alone isn't enough: the message must also say what it is. `JSONMarshaler.Marshal` sets that header, which means it only works when the **publisher also uses the CQRS marshaler** (an `EventBus`, or an outbox that marshals with it).

***

## Who Sets `name`? Nobody We Consume From

| Publisher                                     | How it publishes                      | Sets `name`? |
| --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------ |
| note domain events (its own outbox)           | `cqrs.JSONMarshaler`                  | ✅           |
| note integration events (`workspace.deleted`) | `json.Marshal` + `message.NewMessage` | ❌           |
| authorization `IntegrationPublisher`          | `json.Marshal` + `message.NewMessage` | ❌           |
| document (NestJS)                             | `@nestjs/microservices` Kafka client  | ❌           |

With the default config (`AckOnUnknownEvent: true`, kept for backwards compatibility), every billing handler would have **acked and dropped every message** with one log line at info level. Workspace deletions would never cancel the subscription and payer removals would never be noticed. Nothing crashes and no test fails. You would find out when a customer gets charged for a deleted workspace.

With `AckOnUnknownEvent: false` it's loud instead: an error, a nack, and the same message redelivered forever, blocking its partition.

***

## Note Already Knew This

Read note's `controller/event/event.go` closely and the split is already there:

* **Its own domain events** (outbox, CQRS marshaler, `name` set) → `eventProcessor.AddHandler(...)`
* **`document.committed` from NestJS** (no `name`) → plain `router.AddConsumerHandler(...)` with a hand-written `json.Unmarshal`

That wasn't an accident: the processor simply can't see foreign messages. Billing has no domain-event outbox at all (its only outbound notification is best-effort), so **every** billing consumer is in the foreign-message case.

***

## The Second Gap: One Consumer Group, Many Topics

Note's controller carries this comment:

```go
// Be careful if we use single subcriber, they will steal each other message
```

One Watermill Kafka subscriber means one `ConsumerGroup`. If three handlers each call `Subscribe` on different topics under the same group, Sarama runs three group members that each subscribe to a different topic. Every member joining or leaving triggers a rebalance of the whole group, which pauses consumption on *all* three topics, and a slow handler on one topic can stall the group's session for the others. Note hit this as "stealing" in practice. Billing therefore creates **one subscriber per handler**, with group `billing-service.<handler>`:

```go
for _, h := range handlers {
    subscriber, err := kafka.NewSubscriber(kafka.SubscriberConfig{
        ConsumerGroup: kafkaCfg.ConsumerGroup + "." + h.name,
        // ...
    }, logger)
    router.AddConsumerHandler(h.name, h.topic, subscriber, h.handler)
}
```

***

## Getting the Typed Handlers Anyway

What we actually wanted from the processor was the typing, not the routing. A small generic helper gives us that without the name check:

```go
// decode turns a typed handler into a router handler. A payload that does not decode is
// logged and acked: retrying cannot fix it, and a nack would block the partition.
func decode[T any](fn func(ctx context.Context, ev *T) error) message.NoPublishHandlerFunc {
    return func(msg *message.Message) error {
        var ev T
        if err := json.Unmarshal(msg.Payload, &ev); err != nil {
            slog.ErrorContext(msg.Context(), "dropping undecodable event", ...)
            return nil
        }
        return fn(msg.Context(), &ev)
    }
}
```

Handlers now read like the CQRS ones:

```go
func (e *Event) roleUpdated(ctx context.Context, ev *share.UserWorkspaceRoleUpdatedEvent) error {
    if ev.Role == share.Owner || ev.WorkspaceId == nil {
        return nil
    }
    return e.app.Cmds.HandlePayerRemoved.Handle(ctx, &app.HandlePayerRemoved{...})
}

router.AddConsumerHandler("role-updated", component.TopicRoleUpdated, sub, decode(e.roleUpdated))
```

There's one deliberate difference from note: a **malformed payload is logged and acked**, not returned as an error. A JSON error is permanent, and Watermill's Kafka subscriber redelivers a nacked message until it succeeds. Since billing has no poison queue, returning the error would freeze the partition behind one bad message. Errors from the command itself (Stripe down, database down) are still returned, so the retry middleware and redelivery handle them.

***

## If We Ever Want the EventProcessor for Integration Events

It's possible, but it's a cross-service contract change, not a billing change:

1. Every publisher sets `name` metadata: both Go integration publishers, plus the NestJS producers (as a Kafka header, which Watermill maps to metadata).
2. The value must equal what the consumer's marshaler generates. `JSONMarshaler` defaults to the Go struct name (`cqrs.FullyQualifiedStructName` or `StructName`), so a TypeScript producer would have to emit `share.UserWorkspaceRoleUpdatedEvent`. That leaks Go naming into the contract, unless we set `GenerateName` on both sides to the topic name.
3. Document it in `api/share/` next to the payload schemas, because a publisher that forgets it fails silently (see above).

Until a consumer needs to fan out on event type inside one topic, the topic already is the type, and the plain router plus `decode[T]` is the simpler contract.

***

## Takeaways

* Watermill's CQRS `EventProcessor` routes on the **`name` metadata**, not just the topic. Messages from publishers that don't use the CQRS marshaler are acked and dropped by default.
* Use the processor for events your service publishes itself through the CQRS marshaler. Use `router.AddConsumerHandler` for anything that crosses a service boundary.
* One consumer group per topic handler.
* Decode errors are permanent: log and ack. Handler errors are transient: return them.

# Limitations

Known capabilities and deployment scenarios the project does not currently support.
These constraints may change as the project and its dependencies evolve.

* [Kubernetes deployment](./kubernetes-deployment)
* [Document replica events](./document-replica-events)

url: /notopia/pr/428/developer/limitations/kubernetes-deployment.md

# Kubernetes deployment limitations

Chart rendering and unit tests do not establish that deployments, upgrades, or identity boundaries
are safe. Complete the following checks on the intended cluster and built images before deployment.

* **Authorization seeding:** policy loads at startup. A pre-install/upgrade hook orders seeding
  before new workload resources but does not stop old pods or prevent concurrent policy writers.
  Follow the downtime-requiring external seed procedure in the
  `deploy/k8s/charts/authorization/README.md` for installs,
  upgrades, and rollbacks. On failed upgrades keep traffic blocked and controllers suspended
  until version-matched manual recovery; generic automatic rollback is unsafe. The chart cannot
  verify external seeding occurred. A future design must address rollout, rollback, and concurrency.
* **Edge trust boundary:** implement and independently verify a non-bypassable identity-header
  boundary and prevent direct downstream access. NetworkPolicy and acknowledgement flags alone
  are not proof. Follow the blockers in the
  `deploy/k8s/charts/notopia-edge/README.md`.
* **Live identity tests:** test direct edge access, alternate routes, spoofed-label pods, all five
  forged identity headers with anonymous and missing-claim tokens, and ordinary versus admin access.
  Test non-Istio mode separately if used; repeat after configuration or infrastructure changes.
* **Live upgrades and gateway:** exercise document and search-worker upgrades, hooks, rollout,
  gateway routing, and health exposure against running workloads on the intended implementation.
* **Image and filesystem:** test all six built service images and their migration/seed hooks with
  the configured UID, GID, filesystem mode, and actual startup dependencies and requests. The
  charts default to UID/GID 1000 and a read-only root, but these have not been validated against
  all images. Use writable volumes for required paths and verify ownership. Hook jobs do not expose
  extra volume mounts; hooks requiring them need a chart change. Root and a writable root filesystem
  are available for trusted debugging, but reduce isolation and do not persist container writes.
* **Web cache:** `.next/cache` is an ephemeral writable volume that masks image contents at that
  path. No explicit ISR configuration was found in the current web source. Verify the built image's
  runtime writes; ISR output can require writable paths outside that mount, including `.next/server`.
* **Document scaling:** see [document replica event delivery](./document-replica-events.md).

For trusted debugging, each service chart accepts:

```yaml
podSecurityContext:
  runAsNonRoot: false
  runAsUser: 0
  runAsGroup: 0
containerSecurityContext:
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
```

These settings also apply to chart hooks. Cluster policy may reject root containers. The filesystem
and process identity are independent; disabling either restriction does not disable the other.

---
url: /notopia/pr/428/developer/limitations/document-replica-events.md
---

# Document replica event delivery

Keep the document service at one replica until event delivery and deletion races are fixed and
verified with multi-replica integration tests. Redis synchronization alone does not solve this.
The chart uses a Recreate deployment to avoid overlapping old and new pods during normal upgrades.

Document pods share a Kafka consumer group, so an event reaches one group member, not every pod.
Each pod owns its own WebSocket connections and loaded documents. Role-change and member-removal
handlers only update or close connections on the pod that receives the event. A user connected to
another pod may retain stale access until their connection is reauthenticated or closed.

When a note is deleted, the document service deletes its associated document row and revisions.
The receiving pod guards its loaded document against further stores, closes its local connections,
and waits for local pending stores before deleting the row. Another pod may miss the event and
subsequently upsert its loaded document, recreating the deleted row. The guard is local memory;
the Hocuspocus Redis extension does not broadcast these application event handlers.

Any fix must deliver revocations and deletion to all relevant live pods and coordinate deletion
with stores across replicas. Test deletion during active edits and in-flight stores, role changes,
member removal, pod restarts, and message delivery failures before allowing scale-out.
